entry.title: Three Ways to Expose SAP Business Capabilities to AI Agents with MCP
entry.content:
If you've been playing with AI agents, you've probably asked yourself this: how do I let an agent find and use real business capabilities without stuffing all the business logic into the prompt? That question is what got me started on this proof of concept. I wanted to explore the question in a practical way, so I built a small insurance-claims scenario and exposed the same business capabilities through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in three different ways: a custom TypeScript MCP server, a CAP-native MCP endpoint, and an MCP server in SAP Integration Suite backed by an API artifact and a destination. I kept the business scenario and data the same across all three approaches—customers, policies, claims, and claim documents—so I could compare the approaches on a consistent basis. In this post, I'll walk through the architecture, some of the interesting implementation details, how I tested the different approaches, and what I learned along the way.

GitHub URL: https://github.com/selvakumar2512/sapmcpserverpoc

A quick disclaimer before we start: this is a technical proof of concept, not a production-ready insurance solution. All the data is synthetic, and the coverage assessment is simple deterministic demonstration logic designed for the POC rather than real-world insurance adjudication.

1. Why compare three MCP patterns?

MCP gives AI applications a standard way to discover and call tools that a server exposes. Building a tool is the easy part. In an enterprise landscape, the more interesting question is where that tool contract should live, and who should own the integration around it.

So I split the experiment into three levels:

  • Level 1 — Custom MCP: How do I build agent tools directly?
  • Level 2 — CAP MCP: How can a CAP service expose its entities and actions through MCP with minimal additional tool code?
  • Level 3 — SAP Integration Suite MCP: How can an enterprise integration layer expose API capabilities as MCP tools for MCP clients?

The idea was simple: keep the business scenario the same and only change how it gets exposed.

2. The insurance-claims scenario

The demo domain has four entities: Customers, Policies, Claims, and ClaimDocuments. My sample claim is CLM100045. It belongs to policy POL1001 and customer CUS1001. It's an accident claim for 8,500, currently sitting in UNDER_REVIEW status. The policy behind it is an active Motor Insurance policy with a deductible of 500.

The claim has three documents attached to it: an Accident Report (received), a Repair Estimate (missing), and a Police Report (missing, but optional). Again, all of this is demo data. No real customers were involved.

Schema

3. Architecture at a glance

Level 1 — Custom MCP

The custom server is written in TypeScript using the MCP SDK. I registered purpose-built tools that fetch claim, policy, customer, and document details, plus two tools that trigger the demo actions.

Level 2 — CAP MCP

Here the CAP service exposes the insurance entities and actions, and the CAP MCP adapter makes them discoverable through an MCP endpoint. The nice part is that you don't have to hand-write a separate tool server for every operation.

Level 3 — Integration Suite MCP

In the third pattern, SAP Integration Suite sits between the MCP client and the CAP service. In my setup, the CAP service and HANA/HDI live in a DEV subaccount, while the Integration Suite API artifact and MCP server live in QA. A destination connects the API artifact to the CAP service.

 

4. Level 1 — Building a custom MCP server

For level one, I built a custom MCP server and registered six tools:

  • get_claim
  • get_policy
  • get_customer
  • get_claim_documents
  • assess_claim_coverage
  • initiate_claim_review

The server uses stdio transport, which works well for local testing with an MCP client or MCP Inspector. The registration flow is very explicit: import each tool's registration function, create the MCP server, register the tools, and connect the stdio transport. That's it.

Server.TS

Each tool module calls the CAP service and returns a structured result. If you're looking at the full repository, I'd recommend reading each tool's input schema and implementation side by side with the server registration so the whole picture makes sense.

4.1. Custom MCP tools in Inspector

  1. Start the Custom MCP server
  • Open Terminal and run: npm start
  • Wait until you see the server startup message: Insurance Claims MCP Server running
  • Keep this Terminal window open. The server needs to keep running the whole time you're using Inspector.
  1. Launch MCP Inspector
  • Open a second Terminal window and run: cd mcp-server and npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector
  • This should launch MCP Inspector and display a local URL in Terminal, typically: http://localhost:6274
  • Open that URL in your browser.

Important: Since the Custom MCP server uses StdioServerTransport, Inspector should start it as a child process using the command and arguments you give it. You usually don't need to start the server separately and then connect to it as an HTTP endpoint.

  1. Connect the Custom MCP server

In MCP Inspector:

  1. Select STDIO as the transport.
  2. Enter the command:          npx
  3. Enter the arguments:         tsx src/server.ts
  4. Set the working directory to your mcp-server folder.
  5. Click Connect.

If the connection succeeds, open the Tools tab and click List Tools.

  1. Verify the six tools

You should see these tools:

 

5. Level 2 — Exposing the CAP service through CAP MCP

At level two, the MCP exposure moves much closer to the domain service itself. The CAP service projects the four insurance entities and declares two actions: assessClaimCoverage and initiateClaimReview.

When I connected to the CAP MCP endpoint locally in Inspector, it exposed three generic operations: describe, query, and call. My test flow was: describe the Claims entity, query the sample claim, describe the action contract, and finally call the action.

  • CAP MCP Inspector session
  1. Start the CAP service
  • Open a new Terminal window and run: cd cap
  • Then start the CAP service: npx cds watch
  • Wait until the CAP service is running on port 4004.
  • Keep this Terminal window open. The CAP service needs to stay running while Inspector connects to it.
  1. Open MCP Inspector
  • Open another Terminal window and run: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector
  • Open the Inspector URL displayed in Terminal.
  • In the left panel, change the Transport Type from STDIO to Streamable HTTP.
  • Enter the following URL: http://localhost:4004/mcp/insurance
  • Click Connect.
  1. List the CAP MCP tools
  • After the connection succeeds:
  1. Open the Tools tab.
  2. Click List Tools.
  3. Confirm that these three tools are visible:
    • describe
    • query
    • call

6. Level 3 — Integration Suite MCP

For level three, I created a destination in Integration Suite that points to the CAP service in DEV. I then built an API artifact on top of that destination and generated an MCP server from the API artifact. The result was an MCP server with read operations for the four entities and POST operations for the two actions.

These are the six tools it generated:

  • get_Claims
  • get_Policies
  • get_Customers
  • get_ClaimDocuments
  • post_assessClaimCoverage
  • post_initiateClaimReview

On the inbound side (QA), I used an OAuth client-credentials flow with the API.invoke scope. The destination used its own, separate client identity on the DEV side to authenticate against CAP. Keeping these two identities apart turned out to be really important, both while setting things up and later while troubleshooting.

The Integration Suite MCP Server takes the capabilities of the underlying API artifact and exposes them as MCP tools. In this POC, that gave me four read operations and two business actions, and I didn't have to write a single MCP tool handler in the agent application to get there.

The Integration Suite MCP Server takes the capabilities of the underlying API artifact and exposes them as MCP tools. In this POC, that gave me four read operations and two business actions, and I didn't have to write a single MCP tool handler in the agent application to get there.

Authentication for the remote MCP endpoint

For the remote Integration Suite MCP endpoint, I went with OAuth 2.0 client credentials. The client gets an access token from the configured authorization service, and I passed that token to MCP Inspector as a bearer token. I've deliberately left out all credentials, tokens, and service-key values from this post.

Next — execute get_Claims

Click the Tools tab at the top.

You should see the six tools:

get_Claimsget_Policiesget_Customersget_ClaimDocumentspost_assessClaimCoveragepost_initiateClaimReview

Select get_Claims.

For its input, use the claim identifier:  CLM100045

Click Run Tool.

Wait for the response to appear. You should see output as below:

7. Authentication and connectivity: what I learned

One of the biggest practical lessons for me was keeping two things clearly separate: the token a client uses to call the QA API/MCP endpoint, and the credentials the destination uses to call the protected CAP service in DEV. They sit on different trust boundaries, and mixing them up will only cause you pain.

While testing in Inspector, connecting directly from the browser to the remote MCP endpoint gave me a not-very-helpful “TypeError: Load failed” error. When I switched the Inspector connection type to Via Proxy, it connected fine. Keep in mind this is what I saw in my environment. It may not apply to every setup.

I also ran into an availability problem: CAP database queries started timing out because HANA had stopped responding. Restarting HANA Cloud fixed it, and the CAP and API calls worked again. It was a good reminder to check each hop on its own. A green status on your application doesn't mean the whole path behind it is healthy.

Here's the cleaned-up MCP Inspector configuration I used for the remote test.

MCP Inspector v1.0.2 

Transport Type  [ Streamable HTTP ] 

URL  https://<integration-suite-host>/mcp/insurance-claims 

Connection Type. [ Via Proxy ] 

Authentication   Custom Headers   

Authorization    [ REDACTED ]  

OAuth 2.0 Flow

 

8. Testing the tools

I used MCP Inspector to check that the tools could be discovered and executed. My main test set covered four read operations and two actions.

Get_Claims:

 

Post_assessClaimCoverage:

Post_initiateClaimReview:

9. What the assessment result means—and does not mean

For the sample claim, the demo action returned POTENTIALLY_COVERED, a claim amount of 8,500, a deductible of 500, a potential payable amount of 8,000, and one missing document: the Repair Estimate.

To be clear, this is not a claim approval, a payment authorization, or a full reading of an insurance contract. The rules are intentionally simple and made up. I also instructed the agent to report what the tools return as-is, without making up currencies or guessing what a missing document might mean for the claim.

10. Results and current boundary

As I write this, the custom MCP and CAP MCP paths are built and tested, and all six Integration Suite MCP tools passed my tests in Inspector. I also verified the full API artifact path, from QA through the destination to the DEV CAP service and HANA/HDI.

What's still left is a complete run from an AI agent to the Level 3 Integration Suite MCP endpoint, including getting and refreshing tokens securely. The Inspector tests show that the MCP server and tools are reachable and working, but I don't want to oversell it: they don't prove the full AI-agent-to-Level-3 workflow is done yet.

 

11. Lessons learned

  • Pick the exposure layer based on where you want the tool contracts, the integration work, and the operational ownership to live.
  • Keep inbound MCP/API authorization and outbound destination authentication clearly apart.
  • Test each hop on its own: CAP directly, then the API artifact, then MCP initialize and tools/list, and only then the individual tool calls.
  • If direct browser access fails in your setup, try Inspector's proxy mode, and write down the exact error message so you can diagnose it.
  • Treat the backend as part of the integration path. A healthy-looking application doesn't guarantee the database is responding.
  • Keep the AI agent grounded in what the tools actually return, and don't let it invent business rules or conclusions.

What this POC does not prove

This POC shows that MCP tools can be exposed, discovered, authenticated, and called across three different implementation patterns. That's all it claims. It isn't a production architecture review, an insurance claims engine, a performance benchmark, a security certification, or a recommendation that one pattern beats the others. Before using anything like this in production, you'd need to test much more: authorization, token lifecycle, observability, resilience, rate limiting, error handling, and backend availability.

12. Limitations and next steps

  • Finish the end-to-end test from the AI agent to the Integration Suite MCP endpoint, and document it.
  • Add secure token refresh and proper credential lifecycle handling on the agent side.
  • Add more negative tests: unknown claim ID, missing policy, invalid action input, expired token, and an unavailable backend.
  • Go through authorization scopes, logging, error handling, monitoring, and rate limits before even thinking about production.
  • Keep the scenario synthetic, and keep labeling the coverage calculation clearly as demo logic.

Conclusion

Building this POC gave me a hands-on way to compare three MCP exposure patterns against the same business scenario. The custom server shows what it looks like to implement every tool yourself. CAP MCP puts the MCP exposure right next to the domain service. Integration Suite MCP adds an integration and managed exposure layer in front of the API. In my environment, the Integration Suite MCP server exposed six API-derived tools and called them successfully against the CAP-backed sample data and actions. Connecting an AI agent to Level 3 is the next step for me, and after that comes the operational and security testing you'd need to take something like this beyond a POC. I hope this helps if you're exploring MCP in your own SAP landscape, and I'd love to hear how you're approaching it in the comments.

entry.title: Beat the Single Exclusive Queue Bottleneck : Key-Based JMS Partitioning in SAP Cloud Integration
entry.content:
Beat the Single Exclusive Queue Bottleneck

Key-based JMS partitioning in SAP Cloud Integration — stay in order and process fast

Every integration developer meets this wall sooner or later: "these messages must be processed in order." The easy fix — a single exclusive queue: one consumer, one message at a time — works perfectly and scales terribly. The moment volume rises, that single ordered lane becomes the bottleneck everything queues behind.

Sound familiar? How many times have you "solved" ordering by throttling everything down to one-at-a-time, then watched the backlog grow?

Here's the good news: you almost never need global order. You need order per key. Once you see that, you can keep strict ordering and run in parallel — on plain JMS, no premium add-ons. Let's build the idea up from scratch.

Think of a supermarket, not a single till

Picture a shop with one checkout. Everyone is served in order — beautifully fair, hopelessly slow. The queue out the door isn't a correctness problem; it's a throughput problem.

Now picture several checkout lanes with one rule: the same shopper always goes to the same lane. Each lane still serves its shoppers strictly in order, but different shoppers check out at the same time. Nobody's order is scrambled, and the shop moves.

That's the whole trick. In messaging terms:

  • the lane = a queue processed one message at a time (in order)
  • the shopper = your business key (here, the production order number)
  • "same shopper, same lane" = route each key to a fixed queue

This has a precise name: key-based partitioning with in-order processing — partition by key so each key always lands on the same queue, then process each queue in order with a single consumer. (Database folks will recognise the mechanism as hash sharding: route a hash of the key to one of N stores. Same idea, applied to queues.)

Why "one exclusive queue" hurts

A single ordered queue (in SAP CPI: a JMS queue with Access Type = Exclusive, one consumer, concurrency 1) serializes everything:

One exclusive queue Key-partitioned queues

Order keptGlobally (whole stream)Per key
ParallelismNone — one at a timeUp to N keys at once
ThroughputFloorN× higher
Backlog headroom1 queue's depthN queues' depth

So ask yourself: do order A and order B actually care about each other? Almost never. Only their own messages must stay sequenced. Global ordering is paying for a guarantee the business didn't ask for.

Taking away the ordering you don't need is the whole optimisation.

The pattern, concretely

Give yourself N queues (partitions) and route by a hash of the key:

partition = floorMod( hash(businessKey), N )
queue     = Q_SITE_<partition>

Because the hash depends only on the key, every message for that key lands on the same partition — and because each partition is drained by a single consumer, those messages are processed strictly in order.

Example with N = 2 (real Java hashCode, then mod 2 — even → 0, odd → 1):

Business keypartitionQueue
PO-10010Q_SITE_0
PO-10021Q_SITE_1
PO-10030Q_SITE_0
PO-10041Q_SITE_1
PO-10050Q_SITE_0

And all of one key's messages ride the same lane, in order:

Messages Key Partition Behaviour

PO-1001 msg 1→5PO-1001Q_SITE_0processed 1→2→3→4→5, no overlap
PO-1002 msg 1→5PO-1002Q_SITE_1runs in parallel with PO-1001

Same shopper, same lane — simple, right?

The ceiling to remember: your number of parallel lanes equals the number of JMS queues you allocate. On JMS, partitions aren't free-floating like Kafka — each partition is a real queue, and a tenant has a finite queue budget. So N = how many keys you want in flight at once, capped by available JMS queues (sizing below).

Making it real in SAP Cloud Integration

Want to see how little code this takes? Two iFlows: a dispatcher that routes each message to its partition, and N consumers that each drain one partition in order.

Dispatcher — HTTPS sender → Content Modifier → Groovy → JMS receiver (dynamic queue).

A Content Modifier first promotes the externalized parameters to exchange properties (Groovy can't read {{...}} parameters directly): set partitionLimit = {{partitionLimit}} and site = {{site}}. Then the Groovy derives the partition and sets the target queue name:

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper

Message processData(Message message) {
    // stream the body so the scanner is happy; stream-caching keeps it readable for the JMS send
    def json = new JsonSlurper().parse(message.getBody(java.io.Reader.class))

    def raw = (json.productionOrder ?: '').toString()
    if (!raw?.trim()) throw new IllegalStateException("productionOrder missing — cannot partition")
    def orderNo   = raw.trim().toUpperCase()                 // normalize -> same key, same partition
    def messageNo = (json.messageNo ?: '').toString().trim()

    // partitionLimit (N) is mandatory — fail loudly if the User didn't set the External Parameter
    def limitRaw = message.getProperty('partitionLimit')
    if (limitRaw == null || !limitRaw.toString().trim())
        throw new IllegalStateException("partitionLimit is empty — set it via External Parameter {{partitionLimit}}")
    int n = limitRaw.toString().trim() as int
    if (n < 1) throw new IllegalStateException("partitionLimit must be >= 1 (its set as ${n})")

    def site      = ((message.getProperty('site') ?: 'SITE') as String).trim().toUpperCase()
    int partition = Math.floorMod(orderNo.hashCode(), n)     // deterministic & stable
    def queue     = "Q_${site}_${partition}".toString()      // underscores only; e.g. Q_SITE_0

    message.setProperty('queueName', queue)                  // JMS receiver Queue Name = ${property.queueName}

    def mpl = messageLogFactory?.getMessageLog(message)
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('orderNo', orderNo)
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('messageNo', messageNo)
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('partition', partition.toString())
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('queueName', queue)
    return message
}

The JMS receiver uses Queue Name = ${property.queueName} (match the capitalisation exactly), Access Type = Exclusive.

Consumer — one per partition (Consumer_SITE_0, Consumer_SITE_1, …). The single setting that creates in-order processing is Number of Concurrent Processes = 1 on the JMS sender adapter.

This consumer iflow is set to throw custom exception/error if the messageNo received in the payload is 3. This is done intentionally to test the exclusivity and negatively test retry case 

How many partitions?

Tempted to spin up one queue per order? Resist it. Two limits get confused:

Limit Meaning Rough size

Transactions per queueHow deep one exclusive queue can get (backlog)150 default, max 500
Number of queuesHow many queues the tenant allows30 default , max 100

A queue is a conveyor belt, not a storage box — thousands of keys flow through a handful of lanes over time. Size N to your peak concurrently-active keys (tens), not your total keys (thousands), within your available JMS queue count.

More lanes than you have concurrent keys is just idle queues. Start small, measure, grow.

See it work

Sample Payload sent from Postman

{
  "productionOrder": "PO-1001",
  "messageNo": "1"
}

Likewise its sent for different productionOrders and the respective related messageNos to it. As per the design until messageNo=3 the partition queue do not get stuck.

Any new messages to this partition gets queued and awaits the stuck message clearance.

However regardless of this stall at Q_SITE_0 other Partitions process messages smoothly



Filter the monitor on a custom header for the key: one key's messages sit on a single queue with non-overlapping timestamps (in order), while a different key runs at the same time on another queue (in parallel). That one screen is the whole argument.

The honest catch: a poison message stalls its lane

Here's the uncomfortable question: when a message simply can't be processed — bad data, a missing lookup — should the line stop, or skip ahead?

On an exclusive partition it stops, by design. The failing message stays at the head of its queue, keeps failing, and the rest of that key's messages wait behind it until someone fixes the data and reprocesses. Crucially, only that one partition stalls — every other key keeps flowing.

Is that a bug? No — it's the guarantee doing its job. Better to halt one order's lane than to halt the only global queue. Just monitor queue depth and keep a reprocessing path ready.

Levelling up

What we hand-built on JMS is exactly what SAP Advanced Event Mesh partitioned queues do natively — set a partition key, and the broker handles ordering, parallel consumers, and rebalancing for you. If AEM is in your entitlement, prefer it. And native parallel Exactly-Once-In-Order is on the Cloud Integration roadmap, which will enable context-based in-order processing, providing fine-grained serialization to avoid bottlenecks due to unrelated messages. Until then, key-based JMS partitioning is the pragmatic path without AEM in landscape.

TL;DR

  • You rarely need global order — only order per key.
  • Partition by key (same key → same JMS queue) and process each queue in order (concurrency 1): ordered and parallel.
  • Parallel lanes = number of JMS queues you allocate; size N to peak concurrent keys, not total volume.
  • Ordering's trade-off: a poison message stalls its own lane — monitor and have a reprocess path.

So — next time someone says "it has to be in order," you've got a better answer than "one at a time." What's the trickiest ordering problem you've had to tame? or Any questions? Tell me in the comments.

Disclosure: I used AI assistance to help draft and structure this post. The design decisions, hands-on build, and testing are my own, and I reviewed and validated the content before publishing.

entry.title: Transport CAP Apps and Integration Artefacts directly from Git with SAP Content Agent Service
entry.content:
We are excited to share the recent capability in the SAP Content Agent service: This feature allows teams to push CAP applications and SAP Integration Suite artefacts (such as SAP Cloud Integration flows, scripts, and related configuration content) from a Git repository, allowing to create transport requests in SAP Cloud Transport Management Service (cTMS). 

Transport SAP Cloud Integration Artefacts from repo using SAP Content Agent service

SAP Integration Suite customers have managed integration artefacts — iFlows, Value Mappings, Message Mappings, and more — entirely within the SAP Integration Suite design-time UI. That works well for small teams. But as integration estates grow, two pain points emerge consistently. 

The new feature solves the problem of no source control for integration content when multiple developers work on the same package, there is no branching, no peer-review process, and no reliable version history. 

  1. We start with a sample source code repository setup which has a folder structure for all the archived content. 
  2. Create a destination to connect to your source code repository directly from the SAP Content Agent service UI.
    Specify the required inputs needed: repo URL, token, and path to archived content. 
  3. Once the setup is completed, you can proceed to browse and select the artefacts and create a new transport request.

Transport build artefacts for CAP-based applications from repo using SAP Content Agent service

Traditionally, the CAP application source code is maintained in repositories like Git, Azure Repos, Gitlabs, etc. The developers can use CAS UI or APIs and embed the transport capabilities in their existing workflows. This is supported for full stack, standalone Html5, App frontend applications.

  2. Add a script in the pipeline to retain the artefacts post build. Sample provided for GitHub Actions pipeline.

    uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
    with:
      name: ${{ steps.build.outputs.mtar_name }} # artifact label = archive name, e.g. capire.bookshop_1.0.0
      path: ${{ steps.build.outputs.mtar_path }} # full path to the .mtar file eg: "mta_archives/*.mtar"


  3. Connect the source code repo in SAP Content Agent service using the setup wizard.
    Specify the required inputs needed: repo URL, token, type as "CAP Application", branch and name for built artefacts as per the pipeline configurations. 
  4. Once the set up is done, proceed to create a transport request.
Watch the complete transport request demo in this youtube video 

Stay tuned for more upcoming features on SAP Cloud Integration Artefacts!

1. Push content to Git

SAP Content Agent service supports two push patterns:

  • Transport ZIP in Git — store the packaged transport archive, or
  • Source files directly — store the content’s source files in a structure organized by package and artefacts.

Both GitHub and Azure Repos are supported. Authentication uses a personal access token (or equivalent repository credentials), and you can specify a target repository path or subfolder. Each push creates a commit with a predefined or supplied message.

2. Synchronise Git changes back to CPI

After an artefact is changed in Git, SAP Content Agent Service scans the repository, identifies the available packages and artefact types, displays the modified files, and synchronizes the selected changes into the connected SAP Cloud Integration instance. In the demonstrated flow, the bundle version advanced (e.g., to 1.0.2), after which the package became available for export.

Conclusion: One Unified Interface, Growing Coverage

The unified interface already supports transport-related SAP Integration Suite and SAP API Management scenarios. The roadmap includes broader coverage with source code repository and additional SAP BTP scenario types — with the goal of managing more content through a single interface.

entry.title: Getting started with Micro-Integrations on Advanced Event Mesh: Access Options & Activation
entry.content:
Not every integration scenario requires a full-fledged integration platform. For some scenarios, all you need is a lightweight way to connect an application or service directly to your event broker.

This is where the Micro-Integrations capability of SAP Integration Suite, advanced Event Mesh comes in.
They provide lightweight integration functionality to easily connect SaaS and legacy applications, LLMs and AI Agents, messaging services, data stores, file servers, etc. directly to your event brokers. It also supports basic transformations, comparable to message mappings.

The keyword here is lightweight. Micro-Integrations are not a replacement for Cloud Integration, it complements it. Cloud Integration is designed to handle integration complexity way beyond the level that the Micro-Integrations capability can handle. Micro-Integrations focus on simplicity, speed, and high volume use cases.

In practice, using Cloud Integration for simple pass-through scenarios from or to Advanced Event Mesh with no transformation (apart from perhaps a message mapping) can be inefficient. In high-volume scenarios (e.g. Event Streaming) it means you’re consuming a lot of messages without leveraging the true strength of Cloud Integration.
This is exactly where the Micro-Integrations capability adds value: handling lightweight, high-throughput integrations, closer to the event broker, while leaving the more complex transformations to Cloud Integration.

The following blog: Small but Great: Introducing Micro-Integrations for Advanced Event Mesh was published when Micro-Integrations were released and provides more background on the capability. I recommend reading it before continuing this blog, as it explains the capability and benefits in more detail, this blog focuses specifically on how to obtain access.

Initially, included with certain broker service classes (as from Broker 1K), now they are also available an an additional chargeable capability. This new metric you can be charged for each hour an additional Micro-Integration is in state "deployed", the pricing can be found on SAP Discovery Center.

The following table shows how many Micro-Integrations (MI) are included with each broker service class, note that each MI can contain up to 5 flows:

Service ClassNr. of Micro-Integrations Included
Broker 100 (Developer)0
Broker 250 (Smallest Production Broker)0
Broker 1K2
Broker 5K5
Broker 10K8
Broker 50K15
Broker 100K25


This new (Micro-Integration by the hour) metric enables organizations to:

  1. Leverage Micro-Integrations when they only have small brokers:
    We recommend having the same broker size for PROD and QA. This means that for a 3 tier environment the smallest setup is Broker 250 for PROD and QA and Broker 100 for DEV. In this case, Micro-Integrations are not included in your broker and if you want to use Micro-Integrations, you need to purchase it as a seperate line item.

  2. Use additional flows:
    Every Micro-Integration comes with 5 flows, a single flow contains the details of a target/source system/queue/topic, error handling config (e.g. Dead Message Queues) and a message mapping.
    So let's say, you have an SFTP source micro-integration, these flows can listen to their own SFTP server or directory/folder and map different objects, for example:
    • 5 flows that listen to the same SFTP server but each to a different directory.
      One listens to the directory /salesorders and maps sales order objects, another one that listens to /businesspartners and maps business partner objects, etc:
      in this case you require 1 Micro-Integration.
    • 5 flows that each listen to a different SFTP server but they both map and publish sales order objects:
      in this case you require 1 Micro-Integration
    • 10 flows that listen to the same SFTP server, but map different objects:
      in this case you require 2 Micro-Integrations
     
  3. Leverage more Micro-Integrations than included in your Broker or Subaccount:
    Micro-Integrations cannot be shared across Subaccounts, so let's say you have a 3 tier environment with a 1K Broker in PROD & QA and a 250 Broker (no MIs included) in DEV, each environment is hosted in a different SAP BTP Subaccount. In this case, you can leverage 2 Micro-Integrations in PROD, 2 in QA (as this is included in your Broker), but if you were to use Micro-Integrations on your DEV Subaccount, you would need to activate the entitlement for additional Micro-Integrations on your DEV Subaccount.
    Following the same example, if you want to use more than 2 Micro-Integrations in your PROD and/or QA environment, you also need to activate the entitlement for additional MIs on your PROD and/or QA Subaccount.


In this blog, we will walk you through the process of enabling the Micro-Integrations add-on within your SAP AEM environment, as well as the activation process of a 1K Broker or larger.

Assigning the entitlements to your SAP BTP Subaccount

In this first part of the blog, we will assign the required entitlements to the SAP BTP Subaccount. Depending on how you want to obtain Micro-Integrations, this can either be the entitlement for the Micro-Integration add-on or an entitlement for a broker service class that includes Micro-Integrations (Broker 1K or larger).
This part of the process needs to be done by the Subaccount or Global Account Administrator on SAP Business Technology Platform.

  1. Go to your SAP BTP Cockpit
  2. Navigate to the SAP BTP Subaccount, where you have deployed an Advanced Event Mesh environment and where you want to enable Micro-Integrations.

     

  3. In your Subaccount, go to "Entitlements", and click on "Edit".

     

  4. Now, click on "Add Service Plan" on the right top of the table.
  5. Look for "integration-suite-advanced-event-mesh". 
  6. Now you should see "SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh", under "Services available to this subaccount", select this service.

     

  7. Under "Available Plans", select "micro-integration-add-on". This entitlement allows you to create additional Micro-Integrations beyond those included with eligible broker service classes.
  8. Optional: If you want to use the Micro-Integratoins included with your broker service, select the appropriate broker entitlement instead. For example, a Broker 1K includes two Micro-Integrations (this is smallest broker that includes MIs) , please have a look at the documentation if you want to know how many Micro-Integrations are included in your broker.
    You can also assign both entitlements if you want to use the Micro-Integrations included with your broker service and additional Micro-Integrations through the add-on.

     

  9. Once you've selected the right service plans, click on "Add Service Plans" at the bottom of your screen.

     

  10. Don't forget to press the "Save" button.

     

     

Optional: Ensure a compatible broker is available

To deploy Micro-Integrations, you need at least one active broker in your Advanced Event Mesh environment. If you are using the Micro-Integrations included with a broker service, the minimum service class is Broker 1K. If you are using the micro-integration-add-on entitlement, any broker service class can be used. This section is written for organizations that want to deploy a broker that already includes Micro-Integration. The following steps are performed by the Mission Control Manager in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh.

  1. In your SAP BTP Subaccount, go to "Instances and Subscription" and open "SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh" (under "Subscriptions").

     

  2. Now, you are redirected to what we refer to as the “Cloud Console” in Advanced Event Mesh (you can always go back to the cloud console by clicking on the SAP logo on the top left).
  3. In the Cloud Console, scroll down to "Mission control" and open "Cluster Manager".

     

  4. In the Cluster Manager you seee an overview of your existing brokers. If you don't have a 1K Broker or a larger broker, click on "Create Service" on the right top.
  5. Provide at least the following:
    • Service Name
    • Cloud provider & region
    • Service Type: Enterprise
    • Service Class: Broker 1K (or larger)
  6. Click on "Create Service". 

     

  7. Once the service is ready, you should see a screen that looks like this (see screenshot below). This means that your broker was successfully created!

Granting access to Micro-Integrations

If you (or your admin) have successfully configured the appropriate Micro-Integration entitlement and/or broker service, we're almost ready to create and deploy Micro-Integrations. The only thing you must verify is that you and/or the people who should create and deploy the MIs, have the "Micro-Integrations Manager" role assigned. This part of the process is done by the Account Administrator in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh.

  1. In the Cloud Console, click on the user icon (bottom left corner) and go to "Account Details".
  2. Now, go to "User Management" ➡️ "Users", click on the 3 dots right next to the user you want to grant access to Micro-Integrations and hit "Edit".

     

  3. Go to the line "Micro-Integrations" and open the drop-down list, select "Micro-Integrations Manager", and press "Save". Now this user will be able to create and deploy Micro-Integrations in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. Repeat the previous 3 steps to give access to other users.

     

Discovering and creating Micro-Integrations

Once the appropriate entitlement has been assigned, a compatible broker is available, and the Micro-Integrations Manager role has been assigned to your user, you can create and deploy Micro-Integrations.

  1. In the Cloud Console in Advanced Event Mesh, you should now see a tile with the title "Micro-Integrations". Click on this tile.

     

  2. Here, you will find an overview of all Micro-Integrations that are created. Click on "Create Micro-Integration" on the right top.

     

  3. Now, you see an overview of all Micro-Integrations that you can create and configure with Advanced Event Mesh.

     

  4. From this list, you can select a Micro-Integration that fits your use case and start configuring it. Configuring a Micro-Integration is very straight forward, you need the connection and credential details of the source or target system, as well as the queue/topic and broker credentials to create and configure the Micro-Integration.

If you want to try-out a Micro-Integration, I recommend to go through a blog I wrote earlier this year:
File to Mesh: Liberating SFTP Data with Micro-Integrations. 
In this blog, we create a Micro-Integration that listens to an SFTP server and publishes the lines of a CSV file one by one as (mapped) events to the broker. The File to Mesh use case is one where Micro-Integrations are commonly used.

entry.title: MCP and SAP Integration: Connecting AI Agents with Enterprise APIs
entry.content:
Introduction:

AI Agents and MCP are becoming common topics in Enterprise technology discussion. As someone working in SAP Integration , I started wondering how these new technologies fit into the integration patterns , we already use everyday.

One question especially caught my attention : 

Why MCP becoming important for AI Driven Enterprise Integration :

APIs have been the foundation of enterprise integration for many years. We use them to connect applications, exchange data , expose business capabilities , and integrate SAP systems such as SAP S/4 HANA , SAP SuccessFactors, SAP Ariba and SAP Customer Experience solutions with external applications.

But AI brings a new way of interacting with those systems . MCP helps AI Agents to discover and use available tools in a consistent way.

Can an AI Agent use an API : 

Yes, it can. An AI Agent can absolutely call an API.

The difference is in how the API is discovered and used.

In a traditional API integration, the application usually already knows which API to call, where the endpoint is, what parameters it needs, and how to handle the response.

With an AI Agent, the interaction can be more dynamic. For example, a user might simply ask:

“Can you check the status of my latest sales order?”

The agent needs to understand the request, figure out which tool or business capability can help, provide the right information, and then use the result to respond to the user.

This is where MCP (Model Context Protocol)  becomes useful. MCP provides a standardized way for AI agents to discover and interact with available tools and services, rather than requiring every AI use case to be built around a specific API from the start.

 

1.  MCP Meets SAP Integration: Where Does It Fit? : 

MCP does not replace APIs or the integration technologies we already use. Instead, it can act as a bridge between AI Agents and the business capabilities that are already exposed through APIs and integration flows.

Let's take a simple example :

If any a procurement manager asking 

“Which purchase orders are still waiting for approval?”

The AI Agent needs to understand the request and find the right business capability to answer it. With MCP, that capability can be exposed as a tool that the AI Agent can discover and use, without the agent having to deal with all the underlying API details.

Behind the scenes, SAP Integration Suite can continue doing what it already does well-connecting systems, transforming data, managing security, monitoring integrations, and working with APIs.

In this way, MCP doesn't replace the existing SAP integration landscape. Instead, it can add an AI friendly layer on top of the SAP Integration landscape , making existing business capabilities easier for AI Agents to discover and use.

 

 

2. How AI Agents Work: LLMs, Tools, and SAP Joule :  LLM ( Large Language Model)

The AI Agents that helps understand natural language requests and generate responses.

 

 

In SAP world , Joule is a good example of how SAP is bringing AI into business process. Instead of navigating through several screens , users can interact with SAP applications using natural language.

This is where MCP can add value. MCP provides a standard way for an AI agent to discover and use available tools . These tolls can then connect to SAP business capabilities through APIs and Integration services.

3. How MCP and APIs work together in SAP Integration :

As an SAP Integration consultant, I kept wondering how AI agents and MCP fit into the integration patterns we use every day. APIs have long been the foundation of enterprise integration, connecting S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba  with the wider landscape. But AI brings a new way of using those systems.

A simple SAP example:

  • APIs are the individual capabilities: Business Partner, Product Availability, Sales Order, Billing Document. Each one has its own defined interface.
  • MCP is the assistant that knows which ones to use : Ask “Check if 50 units of pump P-100 are available for customer ABC Corp and create a sales order,” and the agent finds the customer, checks stock and creates the order, using the right APIs in the right order.

Today, a developer hard-codes that sequence in an app or iFlow. With MCP, AI agents discover available tools at runtime and use them. Those tools wrap the APIs we already have, and our security and monitoring stay in place.

AI agent → MCP server → API Management + Integration Suite → SAP systems.

4. What about Monitoring , Traceability and Scalability : 

As we have seen, MCP can help AI Agents discover and use business capabilities through APIs and SAP Integration Suite. But as organizations start introducing more AI Agents and connecting them to more SAP business processes, a new challenge emerges:

How do we scale these interactions and still keep track of what each AI Agent is doing?

This is where Scalability and Traceability become important.

Imagine an enterprise has several AI Agents — one helping with procurement, another supporting finance, another helping customer service, and another working with HR processes.

Each of these agents may use different tools and connect to different SAP systems, APIs, and integration flows.

At a small scale, this may be relatively easy to manage. But as the number of agents and requests grows, things can become much more complicated.

For example, if a Finance Agent makes a request and something goes wrong, an integration team may need to understand:

  • Which AI Agent made the request?
  • Which MCP tool did it use?
  • Which API and SAP system were called?
  • Where did the request fail?
  • How long did it take?
  • Can we trace the request from start to finish?

From an SAP Integration Suite perspective , these are not completely new challenges. Monitoring, logging, error handling, and API management are already part of enterprise integration.

As AI Agents grow, we need to know who called what , when and what happened . MCP helps AI Agents discover and use business capabilities, while SAP Integration Suite continues to provide the security , monitoring , governance and scalability needed to manage these interactions.

5. MCP : Latency and Performance :

If MCP makes it easier for AI Agents to discover and use APIs and SAP business capabilities, we also need to think about how quickly those interactions happen. An AI Agent may need to go through MCP, call an API, and then reach an SAP system before it can provide an answer.

For a simple request, this may not be a concern. But if the agent needs to use multiple tools , APIs or SAP systems to complete one request, the response can take longer. That is why, along with making APIs and SAP capabilities easier for AI Agents to use, we also need to consider Latency and Performance . The goal is to make the integration easy for the AI Agent to use , but also efficient enough to provide a good user experience .

6. Security :

Now what about the security with MCP :

MCP can make it easier for AI Agents to discover and use business capabilities through APIs. But in an enterprise environment, easy access should not mean unlimited access.

An AI Agent may be allowed to check an invoice status , but should it also be allowed to approve or pay invoice ?

So, when using MCP with SAP and APIs, we need to think about:

  • Authentication – Who is making the request?
  • Authorization – What is the AI Agent allowed to do?
  • Data protection – What business data can the agent access?
  • API security – How are the underlying APIs protected?
  • Audit and monitoring – Can we see what the AI Agent accessed or changed?

MCP can open the door for AI Agents to interact with enterprise systems, but who gets the keys ? Security and authorization determine which data an agent can access and which actions it is allowed to perform.

6. Wrapping Up :

MCP does not replace APIs or SAP Integration Suite. Instead, it adds an AI friendly Layer that helps AI Agents discover and use existing business capabilities.

As enterprises move toward AI-driven integration, the focus is not only on connectivity, but also on performance, security , governance and scalability.

The real opportunity is to build on the integration landscape we already have and make it ready for AI driven business Interactions.

“We’ve talked about who gets the keys. In Part 2, I’ll show you how to build the lock, with an MCP server on SAP BTP secured by API Management.”

SAP S4HANA ,SAPBTP , IntegrationSuite , CleanCore , EnterpriseArchitecture , SAPArchitecture , APIManagement ,  CloudArchitecture , DigitalTransformation , SAPIntegration.

 

Himani Arya 

SAP Integration Developer

entry.title: How to See Content of a TPZ File?
entry.content:
As more organizations move from SAP PI/PO toward SAP Integration Suite, one of the first challenges during migration is understanding what already exists in the legacy integration landscape.

In an ideal scenario, we still have access to the original SAP PI/PO development system and can inspect the Enterprise Services Repository directly.

In practice, this is not always the case.

Sometimes we only have exported TPZ files. In other situations, we need to analyze a large number of historical mappings without continuously navigating through the original PI/PO system.

This was the motivation behind a small project I started for my own analysis work:

Open Tpz Master

Open Tpz Master is an open-source desktop application designed to analyze SAP PI/PO TPZ exports and make their Message Mapping structures easier to understand outside the original SAP environment.

The Problem

A TPZ export can contain valuable information about PI/PO design-time objects.

However, having the TPZ file is very different from having a convenient way to understand its contents.

This becomes particularly noticeable with Message Mappings.

A mapping may contain:

  • source and target fields

  • standard mapping functions

  • constants

  • nested functions

  • conditions

  • context operations

  • user-defined functions

  • Java code

  • multiple levels of function arguments

When analyzing an unfamiliar interface, understanding these relationships manually can take significant time.

The problem becomes even more relevant during PI/PO to Integration Suite migrations.

Before rebuilding an integration, we normally need to answer questions such as:

  • What does this mapping actually do?

  • Which source fields are used?

  • Which functions are applied?

  • Are User Defined Functions involved?

  • How complex is the mapping?

  • Which schemas are used?

  • Which parts can be migrated directly?

  • Which parts may require redesign?

This led me to experiment with parsing the exported mapping artifacts directly.

Introducing Open Tpz Master

Open Tpz Master reads a TPZ export and extracts supported Message Mapping information from it.

The basic workflow is:

TPZ Export
    |
    v
Extract Mapping Artifacts
    |
    v
Parse Mapping Metadata
    |
    v
Discover Mapping Bricks
    |
    v
Build Mapping Tree
    |
    v
Visualize Mapping Logic

The important point is that this analysis happens locally.

The tool does not require a connection to the original SAP PI/PO system.

Discovering Message Mappings

After loading a TPZ file, Open Tpz Master searches the exported content for supported Message Mapping artifacts.

Detected mappings are displayed in the application.

The user can select an individual mapping and inspect the metadata extracted from the TPZ.

This is useful when a TPZ contains multiple mappings because the archive can be explored without manually navigating through its internal XML structures.

Visualizing Mapping Logic

The part I found most useful during development was converting the mapping definition into a visual structure.

Instead of displaying only the raw mapping XML, Open Tpz Master builds a top-down brick tree representing the mapping logic.

A simplified example could look like this:

Target
  |
  if
  |
  +-------------------+
  |         |         |
  |         |         |
  UDF    stringEquals Source
            |
       +----+----+
       |         |
      trim      const
       |
  mapWithDefault
       |
     Source

Each node represents a mapping brick.

Depending on the mapping, a brick may represent:

  • Source

  • Target

  • Function

  • Constant

  • User Defined Function

  • Mapping operation

The tree makes the relationship between nested mapping functions much easier to inspect.

This is especially helpful when several functions are nested inside one another.

Inspecting Mapping Bricks

Selecting a brick in the graph displays additional information about it.

For example, for a function the tool can expose information such as:

Name:     readRefreshToken
Type:     udf
Category: function
UUID:     brick_5

Function arguments and other available metadata can also be inspected.

This allows the graph to remain relatively simple while detailed technical information is available when required.

User Defined Functions

User Defined Functions are particularly interesting during migration analysis.

Standard graphical mapping functions are usually relatively straightforward to understand.

A UDF can contain arbitrary Java logic.

For this reason, simply knowing that a UDF exists is often not enough.

Open Tpz Master can identify supported UDF definitions and display the associated Java implementation when it is available in the exported mapping metadata.

For example, selecting a UDF node can expose the corresponding implementation in a separate details panel.

This can help answer an important migration question:

Is this mapping purely graphical, or does it contain custom Java logic that needs additional analysis?

Raw Metadata

During development I intentionally kept access to the underlying metadata available.

Although the visual representation is more convenient for normal analysis, sometimes it is necessary to understand exactly how a particular mapping element is represented in the TPZ export.

For this reason, the application can also expose the relevant raw XML metadata.

This has also been useful while improving the parser itself.

 

Why Offline Analysis?

One design decision was important to me from the beginning:

TPZ analysis should be possible completely locally.

Integration artifacts may contain information about customer landscapes, interface structures and custom business logic.

For consultants working with customer systems, uploading these artifacts to an external analysis service may not always be acceptable.

Open Tpz Master therefore performs the analysis on the local machine.

No SAP system connection is required for the core TPZ analysis.

Why Open Source?

The first version of Open Tpz Master is being developed as an open-source Community Edition.

There are several reasons for this.

First, TPZ files come from many different PI/PO systems and releases. Real-world mappings are much more diverse than the examples available during development.

Community feedback can therefore help identify:

  • unsupported mapping structures,

  • unusual function combinations,

  • parsing problems,

  • visualization problems,

  • differences between PI/PO versions.

Second, integration artifacts can contain sensitive information.

For a local analysis tool, being able to inspect the source code can provide additional transparency about how files are processed.

Finally, I would like the initial version to be useful by itself rather than simply being a demonstration.

Current Scope

The initial Community Edition focuses primarily on:

  • TPZ file analysis

  • Message Mapping discovery

  • Message Mapping metadata extraction

  • graphical mapping analysis

  • top-down brick-tree visualization

  • standard mapping function inspection

  • User Defined Function inspection

  • Java UDF code inspection where available

  • raw mapping metadata inspection

  • XSD extraction

  • local/offline processing

The project is still under development, so compatibility with every possible PI/PO mapping structure should not yet be assumed.

Where This Could Go Next

There are several directions I am currently investigating.

One obvious area is improving Message Mapping analysis itself.

Other potential areas include:

  • Mapping comparison

  • Function Library analysis

  • Java Mapping analysis

  • XSLT analysis

  • Communication Channel analysis

  • cross-object dependency analysis

  • where-used analysis

  • complexity scoring

  • automated technical documentation

  • PI/PO to Integration Suite migration assessment

However, I do not want to build these features based only on assumptions.

One of the reasons for publishing the project is to understand which capabilities SAP integration consultants actually find useful.

A Bigger Goal: Migration Analysis

Longer term, I think TPZ analysis can be useful beyond simply displaying Message Mappings.

Consider a migration assessment where an analyzer could identify something like:

Interface
│
├── Message Mapping
│   ├── 37 field mappings
│   ├── 12 standard functions
│   ├── 3 UDFs
│   └── 1 Function Library dependency
│
├── Communication Channel
│   └── SOAP
│
└── Migration Assessment
    ├── Standard mapping: compatible
    ├── UDF: review required
    ├── Java dependency: detected
    └── Estimated complexity: Medium

This is not the current scope of the Community Edition, but it represents an interesting direction for future development.

Instead of simply asking:

"What objects exist in this TPZ?"

we could eventually ask:

"What will I need to consider when migrating these objects?"

That is where I believe this type of tooling could become particularly useful for PI/PO migration projects.

Feedback from the SAP Integration Community

The project is still evolving, and feedback from people working with real SAP PI/PO landscapes would be extremely valuable.

I am particularly interested in hearing about:

  • mapping structures that are difficult to analyze,

  • TPZ files that behave differently from expected,

  • functions that are not represented correctly,

  • information you normally need during migration analysis,

  • features that would save time during PI/PO projects.

Bug reports and feature requests will be managed through GitLab Issues.

When sharing examples publicly, please make sure that TPZ files, XML, screenshots and schemas do not contain confidential customer information.

Sanitized or synthetic examples are preferable.

Conclusion

Open Tpz Master started from a relatively simple requirement:

I have a TPZ file. How can I understand the Message Mapping without having the original PI/PO system available?

That gradually turned into parsing mapping structures, reconstructing function relationships, visualizing them as trees, inspecting UDFs and extracting schemas.

There is still a lot that can be improved.

But I believe TPZ exports contain enough information to make offline analysis useful, particularly as more PI/PO landscapes move toward SAP Integration Suite.

I am publishing the Community Edition to see whether other SAP integration consultants encounter the same problems and, more importantly, what they would expect from such a tool.

Feedback and contributions are welcome.

Project: Open Tpz Master
License: Apache License 2.0
Platform: Desktop / Python / PySide6
Repository: GitLab
Primary Focus: SAP PI/PO TPZ and Message Mapping Analysis
