entry.title: SAP API Management–Part 5: Advanced Topics Routing, Developer Hub, Analytics & MCP Gateway
entry.content:
SAP API Management for Beginners – Part 5: Advanced Topics — Routing, Path Removal, Developer Hub, Analytics & MCP Gateway

Part 5 of a 5-part beginner series on SAP API Management within SAP Integration Suite.

A quick recap

Over Parts 1–4, we went from zero to a fully governed API:

Part What we built
1APIM concepts + complete features tour (with real exported XML)
2Northwind_API_V1 proxy — 75 resources, conditional flows, defaultRaiseFaultPolicy
3VerifyAPIKey + Product/Subscription + Debug + Versioning + Policy Templates
4OauthService proxy (APIM-native token generation) + OAuth validation + KVM + Spike Arrest + Quota + JSON Threat Protection + CORS

By the end of Part 4, the Policy/ folder in our exported proxy has 9 XML files, the Proxy Endpoint PreFlow has 5 policy steps, and the Target Endpoint PreFlow has 2 steps (for S/4HANA scenarios).

In this final post, we tackle the patterns that separate beginners from practitioners:

  1. Routing using policies — send requests to different backends dynamically
  2. Path removal and rewriting — clean consumer-facing URLs
  3. Developer Hub — the consumer's self-service perspective
  4. Analytics dashboards — built-in + custom metrics with Statistics Collector
  5. MCP Gateway — expose your APIs as governed MCP servers for AI agents

1. Routing using policies

In a real-world scenario, you often need a single proxy to route requests to different backends based on conditions — URL path, headers, or consumer identity.

1.1 The use case

Say your organization has two environments:

  • Standard consumers → route to the Northwind V2 service
  • Premium consumers → route to a newer V4 service or a dedicated backend

Or: route /customers/* to one backend and /orders/* to another.

1.2 Route Rules in the Proxy Endpoint

Our Northwind_API_V1 proxy has one route rule — all traffic goes to the default Target Endpoint:

 
xml
<routeRules>
    <routeRule>
        <name>default</name>
        <targetEndPointName>default</targetEndPointName>
        <sequence>1</sequence>
    </routeRule>
</routeRules>

You can define multiple Target Endpoints and use Route Rules with conditions to select between them:

 
xml
<routeRules>
    <routeRule>
        <name>premium-route</name>
        <targetEndPointName>PremiumBackend</targetEndPointName>
        <conditions>apiproduct.name = "Premium_Product"</conditions>
        <sequence>1</sequence>
    </routeRule>
    <routeRule>
        <name>default-route</name>
        <targetEndPointName>default</targetEndPointName>
        <sequence>2</sequence>
    </routeRule>
</routeRules>

The first rule that matches wins. Premium consumers (subscribed to Premium_Product) get routed to PremiumBackend. Everyone else falls through to default.

1.3 Dynamic routing with Assign Message

A simpler approach: use an Assign Message policy on the TargetEndpoint PreFlow to dynamically change the target URL at runtime.

Where: TargetEndpoint → PreFlow → Incoming Request

 
xml
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" 
               enabled="true" 
               xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <AssignVariable>
        <Name>target.url</Name>
        <Value>https://alternative-backend.example.com/api</Value>
    </AssignVariable>
</AssignMessage>

This overrides the target URL for every request. More useful with a condition — route based on a header, query parameter, or the consumer's product tier.

💡Routing at the gateway level is what makes APIM an integration layer, not just a proxy. Instead of building routing logic in CPI or in the consumer's code, you handle it at the gateway — centralized, visible, and configurable without code changes.

 

2. Path removal and rewriting

This is one of the most common real-world patterns. Your backend has long, complex paths, but you want consumers to call clean, short URLs.

2.1 The problem

Your S/4HANA OData service lives at:

 
https://my12345.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner

You want consumers to call:

 
https://<apim-host>/partners

2.2 Path rewriting with Assign Message

Where: TargetEndpoint → PreFlow → Incoming Request

Step 1: Set your proxy's API Base Path to /partners.

Step 2: Add an Assign Message policy to rewrite the path:

 
xml
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" 
               enabled="true" 
               xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Set>
        <Path>/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner</Path>
    </Set>
    <AssignTo createNew="false" type="request"/>
</AssignMessage>

Now when a consumer calls GET /partners?$top=5, APIM translates it to the full S/4HANA path before sending it to the backend.

2.3 Path prefix removal with JavaScript

For more dynamic path manipulation — stripping a prefix, appending a suffix, or transforming the path based on variables — use a JavaScript policy:

Step 1: Add a JavaScript policy to TargetEndpoint PreFlow:

 
xml
<Javascript async="false" continueOnError="false" 
            enabled="true" 
            xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <ResourceURL>jsc://removePathPrefix.js</ResourceURL>
</Javascript>

Step 2: Upload the JavaScript file as a proxy resource (removePathPrefix.js

 
javascript
var originalPath = context.getVariable("proxy.pathsuffix");
// Strip the versioned prefix
var newPath = originalPath.replace("/api/v1", "");
context.setVariable("target.copy.pathsuffix", false);
context.setVariable("target.url", 
    context.getVariable("target.url") + newPath);

💡Path removal is about consumer experience. Your consumers shouldn't need to know your backend's internal URL structure. Give them clean, versioned, RESTful paths — let APIM translate behind the scenes.

⚠️Test path changes with the Debug tool. A missing or extra / in the path rewrite is the most common cause of 404 errors. Debug shows you the outbound request URL — verify it matches what the backend expects.

 

3. Developer Hub — the consumer's perspective

We've been working in the API Portal (admin side). The Developer Hub is what your consumers — partner developers, mobile teams, third-party integrators — actually see.

3.1 What consumers see

Section Content
Home pagePublished Products as cards with descriptions, API counts, and quota info
Product detailAPIs included, quota limits, documentation links
API detailAll resources (from the Resource tab), parameters, example responses
Try Out consoleEmbedded API test tool — send real requests from the browser without Postman
My ApplicationsConsumer's own Applications with API keys and usage stats

 

3.2 The consumer journey

  1. Discover — browse Products, read descriptions, explore API resources
  2. Try Out — test APIs directly in the browser console (no Postman needed)
  3. Subscribe — pick a Product, create an Application, get API key + secret
  4. Build — use the key in their integration
  5. Monitor — check their own usage and remaining quota in the portal

💡The Try Out console is a game changer for developer experience. Instead of emailing API docs, consumers test your APIs live in the browser. The console auto-fills the base URL, handles auth — they pick a resource, add parameters, and hit Send. For our Northwind_API_V1, all 75 resources appear in the console, organized and ready to test.

 

3.3 Self-registration for external consumers

For external developers, enable Self-Registration in Developer Hub settings:

Setting Recommended
Approval required✅Yes (for production) — admin reviews each registration
Email verification✅Yes
Auto-approveOnly for trial/sandbox environments

3.4 Application lifecycle management

From the admin side (API Portal → Manage → Applications

Action When
View all ApplicationsSee who's subscribed and which Products they use
Suspend an ApplicationTemporarily block access — key immediately invalidated, reversible
Revoke an ApplicationPermanently block — consumer needs a new Application and key
View usageSee call counts per Application

⚠️The "unidentified application" pattern: If you see traffic from "Unidentified" in Analytics, it means requests are reaching your proxy without being associated with a registered Application. This could mean VerifyAPIKey is disabled or has continueOnError="true" — check your policy config.

4. Analytics dashboards

4.1 Built-in analytics

Go to Analyze APIs from the Integration Suite launchpad. Three views:

Overview (Executive view):

KPI What it shows
Total TrafficTotal API calls for the selected period
Average Response TimeMean latency in ms
Total Errors4xx + 5xx count
Top APIs by TrafficMost-called proxies
Top ApplicationsMost active consumers
Slowest APIsProxies with highest latency
Response Code Distribution2xx vs 4xx vs 5xx ratios

 

Health (DevOps view):

Error trends (4xx vs 5xx over time), response time percentiles (P50, P90, P95), error breakdown by proxy and response code.

💡The 401 vs 429 vs 500 breakdown is your diagnostic starting point:

  • High 401 → consumers misconfiguring API keys or OAuth tokens (education problem)
  • High 429 → consumers hitting Spike Arrest or Quota limits (capacity problem)
  • High 500 → backend failing or policy misconfiguration like unresolved KVM variables (infrastructure problem)

Usage (Product Manager view):

Traffic by Product, Application, and Developer. API call distribution across resources.

4.2 Custom dashboards with Statistics Collector

Need to track something specific — like which Northwind Customers are queried most?

Step 1: Add an Extract Variables policy (ProxyEndpoint PostFlow, Outgoing Response):

 
xml
<ExtractVariables async="true" continueOnError="true" 
                   enabled="true" 
                   xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <URIPath>
        <Pattern ignoreCase="true">/Customers('{customerId}')</Pattern>
    </URIPath>
    <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>true</IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>
</ExtractVariables>

⚠️Note continueOnError="true" here. Not every request will match the pattern (list requests don't have a CustomerID in the path). We don't want the policy to fail on non-matching URLs.

Step 2: Add a Statistics Collector policy right after:

 
xml
<StatisticsCollector async="false" continueOnError="false" 
                      enabled="true" 
                      xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Statistics>
        <Statistic name="customerId" ref="customerId" type="string">unknown</Statistic>
    </Statistics>
</StatisticsCollector>

The unknown default is used when the variable isn't resolved (e.g., on a list request).

Step 3: Go to Analyze → dropdown → Custom View → create a chart with customerId as the dimension.

💡This is powerful for business intelligence. Your product owner can see: "Customer ALFKI is queried 500 times a day by the 3PL integration, but BERGS is only queried twice." That's actionable — maybe the 3PL should be caching ALFKI's data.

5. MCP Gateway — expose APIs for AI agents

This is the newest capability in SAP Integration Suite — and the one that positions your APIs for the agentic era.

5.1 What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open standard that lets AI agents discover and call tools at runtime — without hardcoded integrations.

 
Without MCP:  Developer hardcodes API endpoints into agent tool definitions
With MCP:     Agent connects to MCP server → discovers tools from metadata → calls them

Think of MCP as "USB-C for AI agents" — a universal plug that lets any agent connect to any tool server.

5.2 How MCP Gateway works in Integration Suite

The MCP Gateway sits on top of the API proxies we've already built:

 
AI Agent (Claude Desktop / Copilot Studio / Cline / Joule)
    ↓ Streamable HTTP + OAuth Bearer token
MCP Gateway (SAP Integration Suite)
    ↓ All existing policies apply (APIKey, Quota, Spike Arrest, etc.)
API Artifact (Northwind_API_V1 or any managed API)
    ↓
Backend (Northwind / S/4HANA / any system)

All your existing policies still apply — the agent is just another consumer, accessing through MCP instead of direct HTTP. The MCP endpoint follows a standard pattern:

 
https://<your-apim-host>/mcp/v1/<server-name>

5.3 Prerequisites

Prerequisite Details
Integration Suite editionPremium, Enhanced, or Trial (Free Plan)
Capabilities activatedCloud Integration AND API Management
Integration Cell runtimeEnabled and Active (Settings → Runtimes)
RolePI_Integration_Developer assigned to your user

⚠️MCP Servers run on Integration Cell, not the classic Cloud Integration runtime. Go to Settings → Runtimes and confirm Integration Cell shows as Active.

5.4 Three source types for MCP Servers

SAP Integration Suite supports three ways to create an MCP Server:

Source type What it does Best for
APICreate from an existing API artifact deployed on Integration CellOur Northwind proxy — most common
HTTP Endpoint + OpenAPI specImport an OpenAPI specification and expose operations from any HTTP endpointThird-party REST APIs without an APIM proxy
RFCExpose SAP RFC-enabled function modules as MCP toolsDirect S/4HANA or ECC RFC access

We'll use the API approach — creating the MCP Server from our Northwind_API_V1 proxy.

5.5 Create the MCP Server

Step 1: In Integration Suite, navigate to Design → select an Integration Package (or create one).

Step 2: Click Add → MCP Server.

Step 3: Select the source:

Field Value
Source TypeAPI
API ArtifactNorthwind_API_V1

Step 4: Configure the MCP Server details:

Field Value Notes
NameNorthwind_MCPInternal identifier
MCP Path/northwind-toolsUnique path — the full URL becomes https://<host>/mcp/v1/northwind-tools
DescriptionTools to search and retrieve Customers, Orders, and Products from the Northwind demo service. Supports OData filtering, pagination, and entity relationships.Write this for the AI agent — it uses this to decide relevance

⚠️The MCP Path must be unique across all MCP Servers in your tenant. Choose a descriptive, hyphenated name.

5.6 Select and describe tools

The MCP Server auto-discovers resources from your API artifact and presents them as potential tools. You select which ones to expose.

Step 1: Review the discovered resources. For our 75-resource Northwind proxy, you'll see all entity sets, navigation properties, and views.

Step 2: Select the tools to expose. For a beginner setup, start with the core operations:

Tool to expose Source resource Why
GET /CustomersCustomers (collection)List/search customers
GET /Customers('{CustomerID}')Customers (by key)Get a specific customer
GET /Customers('{CustomerID}')/OrdersCustomer's Orders (navigation)Orders for a customer
GET /ProductsProducts (collection)List/search products
GET /OrdersOrders (collection)List/search orders
GET /Orders({OrderID})/Order_DetailsOrder Details (navigation)Line items for an order

Step 3: For each selected tool, write a clear description:

Tool Auto-generated description Your enhanced description
GET /Customers"Retrieves Customers entities""Search for customers by company name, country, or city. Returns CustomerID, CompanyName, ContactName, Address, City, Country. Use OData $filter for specific criteria, e.g., $filter=Country eq 'Germany'"
GET /Products"Retrieves Products entities""List products with name, price, stock level, and category. Filter by price range with $filter=UnitPrice gt 20. Use $top and $skip for pagination"

💡Tool descriptions are the most important part of an MCP Server. The AI agent reads these descriptions to decide which tool to call and how to construct parameters. A vague description means the agent either picks the wrong tool or sends wrong parameters. Write them as if you're explaining the API to a smart colleague who's never seen Northwind.

 

5.7 Deploy and publish

Step 1: Click Deploy. The MCP Server deploys to the Integration Cell runtime.

Step 2: After successful deployment, the MCP Server is available at:

 
https://<your-apim-host>/mcp/v1/northwind-tools

Step 3: Publish to Developer Hub — this makes the MCP Server discoverable alongside your traditional API Products.

 

5.8 Connect Claude Desktop

Configure Claude Desktop to connect to your MCP Server:

 
json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "northwind-tools": {
      "type": "url",
      "url": "https://<your-apim-host>/mcp/v1/northwind-tools",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <oauth-access-token>"
      }
    }
  }
}

The OAuth token comes from the OauthService proxy we built in Part 4 — or from SAP BTP's OAuth endpoint if you're using platform-level auth.

Once connected, test with a natural language query:

User: "Find all customers in Germany"

Claude: calls GET /Customers with $filter=Country eq 'Germany'

"I found 11 customers in Germany. Here are the first few: Alfreds Futterkiste (Berlin), Blauer See Delikatessen (Mannheim)..."

5.9 Connect other MCP clients

The MCP Gateway uses Streamable HTTP as the transport protocol. Any MCP-compatible client works:

Client Configuration
Claude DesktopmcpServers in settings JSON (shown above)
Cline (VS Code)MCP server configuration in Cline settings
Microsoft Copilot StudioMCP Server connection with OAuth 2.0 via Entra ID trust
SAP JouleNative integration — Joule agents can consume MCP servers from Integration Suite directly
Custom agentsAny MCP client library — connect over Streamable HTTP with OAuth Bearer token

5.10 Governance considerations for AI agents

Exposing APIs to AI agents introduces new patterns:

Rate limiting for agents:

AI agents burst faster than humans — "compare customers in Germany vs France" fires two API calls in milliseconds. Consider:

Approach Configuration
Agent-specific ProductCreate a separate Product with higher Spike Arrest limits for MCP Applications
Burst-aware quotaUse type="flexi" instead of type="calendar" for sliding-window quota

Start with read-only access:

For safety, only expose GET operations as MCP tools initially. Enable write operations (POST, PUT, DELETE) only after validating the agent's behavior in a test environment.

⚠️An agent that can read "Get Customers" is useful. An agent that can write "Delete Customer" is powerful — and risky. Start read-only, validate, then gradually expand.

PII protection:

AI agents may send API responses to external LLMs for processing. Consider adding Assign Message policies that strip sensitive fields (bank details, tax IDs) from responses when the request comes from an MCP-registered Application.

SAP's architectural guidance:

Pattern Protocol Use case
Tool consumptionMCPAgent calls your APIs as tools
Agent delegationA2A (Agent-to-Agent)One agent delegates a task to another

MCP Gateway handles the first pattern. SAP's Agent Gateway (for Joule agents) handles the second. Both are complementary.

6. The complete series — what we've built

Layer Component Part
ConceptsAPIM features tour, architecture, real exported XML1
API ProviderNorthwind_API (+ S/4HANA guidance)2
API ProxyNorthwind_API_V1 — 75 resources, conditional flows, versioned2
Method governanceAuto-generated conditional flows + defaultRaiseFaultPolicy (405)2
SecurityVerifyAPIKey + OauthService (APIM-native token generation) + ValidateOAuthToken3, 4
TrafficSpike Arrest + Quota (with dynamic Product limits)4
Payload securityJSON Threat Protection4
Browser accessCORS headers via Assign Message4
Backend authKVM + Basic Authentication (for S/4HANA scenarios)4
GovernanceProducts, Subscriptions, Policy Templates, Versioning3
Advanced routingRoute Rules, Assign Message path rewriting, JavaScript5
Consumer portalDeveloper Hub, self-registration, Try Out console5
AnalyticsBuilt-in dashboards + custom metrics via Statistics Collector5
AI agentsMCP Gateway — MCP Server from API artifact, Streamable HTTP5

Every layer builds on the previous one. The MCP Gateway reuses the same policies — the agent is just another consumer. The Analytics dashboards show MCP traffic alongside traditional API traffic. That's the compounding value of getting the foundation right.

7. Key lessons from this series

Looking back, there are a handful of insights that prevent 80% of beginner mistakes:

ProxyEndpoint vs TargetEndpoint. Consumer-facing policies (auth, throttling, CORS) go on the Proxy Endpoint. Backend-facing policies (KVM, credential injection) go on the Target Endpoint. This is the APIM equivalent of the Event Mesh credential direction insight (Event Mesh key vs CPI runtime key). Once it clicks, everything falls into place.

XML element ordering. APIM enforces strict element order in policy XML. Source before limits in JSONThreatProtection. Allow → Interval → Distributed → StartTime → Synchronous → TimeUnit in Quota. The error messages point to the element that's out of place, not the one that should be there — check the policy template for the correct sequence.

Case sensitivity. The APIKey header is case-sensitive. APIKey ≠ apikey ≠ Apikey. Same gotcha as Event Mesh queue names (3PL vs 3pl).

OAuth body vs headers. client_id and client_secret go in the request body as x-www-form-urlencoded — not in headers. Same as the XSUAA token endpoint in Event Mesh.

Save ≠ Deploy ≠ Version. Save creates a revision (undo). Deploy makes it live. A Version is a separate proxy (V1 → V2). Revisions for iterating, versions for breaking changes.

Conditional flows are free governance. When you create a proxy from an OData service using Discover, APIM auto-generates conditional flows for every resource with HTTP method enforcement. 75 resources × correct method restrictions, generated in one click. Most tutorials make you do this manually.

Quick Reference

Item How
RoutingTarget Endpoint → Route Rules with conditions, or Assign Message to set target.url
Path removalTarget EP PreFlow → Assign Message with <Set><Path>...</Path></Set>
JavaScript policyUpload .js file as proxy resource, reference via <ResourceURL>jsc://filename.js</ResourceURL>
Developer HubIntegration Suite launchpad → Developer Hub tile
Self-RegistrationDeveloper Hub → Settings → Enable
AnalyticsAnalyze APIs → Overview / Health / Usage
Custom DashboardAnalyze → Custom View → Create with Statistics Collector dimensions
MCP Gateway prereqsIntegration Cell Active + Premium/Enhanced/Trial edition + PI_Integration_Developer role
MCP Source typesAPI artifact, HTTP Endpoint + OpenAPI spec, or RFC
MCP Endpointhttps://<host>/mcp/v1/<server-name>
Claude DesktopmcpServers config with type: "url" + gateway URL + OAuth Bearer token

Wrapping up the series

When we started in Part 1, the question was simple: why can't you just give consumers the direct API URL? Five posts later, the answer spans security, traffic management, OAuth token generation, consumer experience, analytics, and AI-agent readiness.

SAP API Management gives you a single governed layer that stacks cleanly:

  • API Provider → connects to the backend once
  • API Proxy → wraps it with policies and conditional flows
  • OauthService → generates tokens without any external IdP
  • Product → packages proxies for different consumer tiers
  • Developer Hub → lets consumers self-serve
  • Analytics → shows you what's happening
  • MCP Gateway → extends everything to AI agents

Everything reuses what came before. The MCP Gateway doesn't need new policies — it uses the same ones. The Analytics dashboards show MCP data alongside traditional API data. The OauthService proxy issues tokens for both human consumers and AI agents.

And every real error we hit during testing — XML element ordering, OAuth body vs headers, KVM variable resolution, case sensitivity — is now documented in the troubleshooting tables. That's the value of building hands-on instead of just reading documentation.

Thank you for following along. If you've built something with this series, I'd love to hear about it in the comments.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 0: The big picture
entry.content:
Part 0 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent. This post is the map; Parts 1 to 7 build it, one piece at a time.

Moving integration content from a development system to the next system sounds simple. In SAP BTP it takes three services, five connections and three kinds of permissions. In my last project, connecting the services took a few hours. Getting the permissions right took days.

This series walks through the setup I built, in plain words. This first post explains the pieces, how they fit together, and the one idea that would have saved me most of those days.

What we move

  • Integration Suite packages: your integration flows and everything that belongs to them.
  • Role collections: bundles of permissions you give to users.
  • Destinations: saved connection details (an address plus how to log in).

The three services, in one sentence each

Think of a transport as sending a parcel.

  • SAP Integration Suite is where developers build. It has a Transport button. That is where the parcel starts.
  • SAP Content Agent service is the packer. It collects the content and packs it into one file, an MTA archive (.mtar). On the other side, a second Content Agent unpacks it.
  • SAP Cloud Transport Management (CTMS) is the delivery service. It never opens the parcel. It moves it from one stop (a node) to the next along a route, and a person with the right permission decides when it is delivered (the import).

The landscape

Everything runs between two subaccounts, and the whole series stays with these two:

  • Dev: where developers build and click Transport.
  • Central: holds the one CTMS for the whole landscape, and the target Integration Suite.

 

 

The five steps in the picture are the whole journey. A developer clicks Transport (1), Content Agent packs the parcel (2), CTMS delivers it (3), someone approves the import (4), and the second Content Agent unpacks it into the target (5).

SAP's tutorials put CTMS in the development subaccount. We put it in Central, so every environment shares one delivery service and Dev only needs a connection to it.

The connections: destinations

Every arrow in the picture is a destination: a saved address plus login details, copied from a service key (the credentials a service gives you). Three of them must have exact names, because Integration Suite looks them up by name: ContentAssemblyService, CloudIntegration and TransportManagementService. Parts 2 and 3 set them up field by field.

The first sign that they work is the Transport setting in Integration Suite:

 

 

The one idea: who is asking?

Almost every error I hit came from giving a permission to the wrong "who". Before you assign anything, ask: is this a service talking to another service, or a person clicking in a screen?

Who is askingWhat it needsWhere you set itWhat you see when it is missing
A service, calling another serviceRoles on the service instanceWhen you create or update the instanceThe transport stops half-way
A person, in a browserA role collection on their userSecurity > Role CollectionsA button or tile is missing
The connection between themA destination with the right credentialsConnectivity > Destinations"Failed to fetch auth token" or "not connected"

Two rules follow from this:

  • A role collection does nothing for a service, and an instance role does nothing for a person.
  • A destination is only as good as the key it was copied from. A wrong client ID or token URL fails quietly until you run a real transport.

Here is what a destination problem looks like. The setting is saved, but the check fails because one destination cannot log in:

 

 

The exact roles are introduced in the part where you need them, and Part 7 collects all of them on one page.

What does not travel

The parcel carries definitions, not secrets. After every import you set these in the target yourself:

  • passwords and client secrets of transported destinations,
  • which users get which role collections,
  • security material (keys and credentials) and values that differ per environment.

The series

PartTopic
0The big picture (this post)
1Central: setting up CTMS, its nodes and the route
2Dev: Content Agent and the three fixed-name destinations
3Central: the second Content Agent and the target
4Switching on Transport and running the first one
5Transporting role collections
6Transporting destinations
7Cheat sheet: every role, where it goes, what breaks without it

Alongside the parts I will publish short Troubleshooting posts, one per error I hit, each linked from the part where it shows up. Links are added here as posts go live.

Before you start

  • Two subaccounts in the Cloud Foundry environment: one for Dev, one for Central.
  • SAP Integration Suite in both, with the Cloud Integration capability switched on.
  • Entitlements for Cloud Transport Management, Content Agent service, Process Integration Runtime and Authorization and Trust Management.
  • Administrator access to both subaccounts.

What comes next. In Part 1 we set up the delivery service, CTMS, in the Central subaccount: subscribing to it, creating the service instance and key, building the source and target nodes, and connecting them with a route. By the end of Part 1 you will have an empty but working transport route, ready for Content Agent to send its first parcel in Part 2.

Does your landscape look different, for example with CTMS in the development subaccount? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: Retrieve Specific User Information from SAP SuccessFactors Using SAP Cloud Integration (OData V2)
entry.content:
Introduction

In many SAP integration scenarios, we need to retrieve information about a specific employee or user from SAP SuccessFactors instead of fetching the entire user dataset.

For example, an external application may send a user ID to SAP Cloud Integration (CPI), and the integration flow must retrieve the corresponding user's details, such as their username, first name, last name, and email address, from SAP SuccessFactors.

In this blog, we will build an integration flow in SAP Integration Suite – Cloud Integration that retrieves user-specific information from SAP SuccessFactors using the OData V2 adapter.

The flow accepts an incoming request, reads the requested user ID, queries the SuccessFactors User entity, processes the response using a Groovy Script, and returns the result to the calling application.

1. Prerequisites

Before implementing this integration flow, ensure that you have the following:

  1. SAP SuccessFactors API access: You must have access to an SAP SuccessFactors environment with API permissions.

  2. SuccessFactors credentials: You need a valid API-enabled user ID and password, along with the appropriate company ID (company code/Company ID used by your SuccessFactors tenant).

  3. SuccessFactors API endpoint: For this example, we will use the following demo endpoint:

    https://apisalesdemo8.successfactors.com

  4. SAP Integration Suite access: You must have access to Cloud Integration and permission to create, configure, and deploy integration flows.

  5. User entity permissions: The SuccessFactors API user must have the necessary permissions to read the User entity and the required fields.

  6. Testing tool: Postman or another HTTP client can be used to send a request to the deployed integration flow.

Important: The demo endpoint is used for illustration. Make sure your tenant, Company ID, credentials, and API permissions are valid before testing. Do not expose passwords or other credentials in the blog or in screenshots.

2. Integration Scenario

The objective is to retrieve information for one specific user based on a user ID supplied in the incoming request.

For example, if the incoming request contains the user ID 100045, the integration flow queries SAP SuccessFactors and returns the matching user's details.

The fields retrieved in this example are:

  • userId

  • username

  • firstName

  • lastName

  • email

Instead of retrieving all users, we use an OData $filter expression to select only the record matching the supplied user ID.

3. Integration Flow Design

Create an integration flow named:

SF_Get_UserSpecific_data

The flow consists of the following main steps:

  1. HTTPS Sender

  2. Content Modifier

  3. Request Reply

  4. SuccessFactors Receiver using the OData V2 adapter

  5. Groovy Script

  6. Message End

The overall processing sequence is:

Incoming HTTP Request → Content Modifier → Request Reply → SuccessFactors OData V2 → Groovy Script → Response

The HTTPS Sender receives the request from the external application. The Content Modifier extracts or prepares the user ID as an exchange property. The Request Reply step invokes SAP SuccessFactors through the receiver channel. After receiving the response, the Groovy Script processes the payload before it is returned to the caller.

IFLOW

 

4. Create the Integration Flow

Log in to SAP Integration Suite and navigate to Design → Integrations and APIs.

Open your integration package or create a new package. Select Add → Integration Flow, provide the name SF_Get_UserSpecific_data, and save it.

Open the integration flow in the editor.

Step 4.1: Configure the HTTPS Sender

Add an HTTPS Sender adapter to the sender participant and connect it to the integration process.

Configure the sender so that an external client can invoke the integration flow through HTTP.

The exact endpoint path and authentication settings depend on your tenant configuration. For production scenarios, configure suitable authentication and authorization.

The calling application will send the user ID in the request payload. We will use that value in the subsequent steps.

 

 

Step 4.2: Configure the Content Modifier

Add a Content Modifier after the Start event.

The purpose of this step is to extract the incoming user ID and store it in an exchange property named userID.

For this example, assume the incoming request is XML:

<UserRequest>
    <userID>10025</userID>
</UserRequest>

If the sender payload is XML, configure the Content Modifier or a preceding transformation step to extract the value using the appropriate XMLPath expression.

For example, where supported by your configuration, use the XMLPath expression:

//userID

Create the exchange property as follows:

Field Value

NameuserID
TypeExpression
Value//userID

The exact expression syntax depends on the Content Modifier field and how the incoming message is represented. If your flow receives XML or plain text instead of JSON, configure the extraction accordingly.

The important result is that the exchange property userID contains the requested user's ID before the Request Reply step is executed.

Note: The SuccessFactors query uses ${property.userID}. Therefore, make sure the property name is exactly userID, including capitalization.

Content Modifier

 

5. Configure the SuccessFactors OData V2 Receiver

Add a Request Reply step to the integration process and connect it to a receiver participant configured with the SuccessFactors adapter.

Create or configure the receiver channel using the SuccessFactors OData V2 adapter.

Step 5.1: Configure the connection

Use the following connection details as a starting point:

Configuration Value

AdapterSuccessFactors OData V2
Address/Service URLhttps://apisalesdemo8.successfactors.com
AuthenticationAs supported and configured for your SuccessFactors tenant
Company IDYour SuccessFactors Company ID
User IDYour API-enabled SuccessFactors user
PasswordThe corresponding password, if required by the selected authentication method

Store credentials securely using the supported security material and authentication configuration in your tenant. Do not hardcode passwords in scripts or expose them in screenshots.

Depending on your adapter configuration, the entity, operation, resource path, and query options may be configured in the receiver channel.

 

Step 5.2: Select the OData entity

For this scenario, use the SuccessFactors User entity.

The User entity provides basic user information, including identifiers and selected personal or contact fields, subject to the permissions granted to the API user.

Configure the operation to read/query the User entity.

Step 5.3: Configure the OData query

Use the following query options:

$select=userId,username,firstName,lastName,email&$filter=userId eq '${property.userID}'

This query contains two important OData options.

$select — Specify the fields to retrieve

$select=userId,username,firstName,lastName,email

This restricts the response to the five fields required for the scenario, rather than requesting every available property.

$filter — Retrieve the matching user

$filter=userId eq '${property.userID}'

This filters the User entity using the userID exchange property populated by the Content Modifier.

If the property contains 100045, the effective filter is:

userId eq '100045'

The resulting query requests only the selected fields for the matching user.

 

6. Add the Groovy Script

-->If you want to log a attachment for the output payload , you can use this groovy script or else just skip the step.

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message

def Message processData(Message message) {

    // Read payload as String
    def body = message.getBody(String)

    // Get Content-Type header
    def headers = message.getHeaders()
    def contentType = headers.get("Content-Type")

    // Default to text/plain if Content-Type is not available
    if (contentType == null || contentType.trim().isEmpty()) {
        contentType = "text/plain"
    }

    // Get Message Processing Log
    def messageLog = messageLogFactory.getMessageLog(message)

    if (messageLog != null) {
        messageLog.addAttachmentAsString("Payload", body, contentType)
    }

    return message
}

 

7. Deploy the Integration Flow

After configuring the sender, Content Modifier, Request Reply, receiver channel, and Groovy Script:

  1. Save the integration flow.

  2. Validate the configuration and resolve any errors.

  3. Configure the required security material and authentication settings.

  4. Deploy the integration flow.

  5. Open the deployed artifact and verify its status.

Once deployed successfully, the HTTPS endpoint can be invoked by an authorized client.

8. Test the Integration Flow Using Postman

Open Postman and create a new HTTP request.

Step 8.1: Configure the request

Use the HTTPS endpoint generated for your deployed integration flow.

Select the HTTP method configured for the sender, typically GET when sending a request body.

Configure the appropriate authentication method for the HTTPS sender and add the content type header:

Content-Type: application/xml

Step 8.2: Send the request payload

In the Body section, select raw → XML and provide:

<UserRequest>
    <userID>10025</userID>
</UserRequest>

Replace 100045 with a valid user ID available in your SuccessFactors tenant.

 

 

Step 8.3: Verify the response

-->My Response from successfactors 

 

Conclusion

In this blog, we explored how to retrieve specific user information from SAP SuccessFactors using SAP Integration Suite – Cloud Integration and the OData V2 adapter.

By combining an HTTPS Sender, Content Modifier, Request Reply, SuccessFactors receiver, and optional Groovy Script, we can build an integration flow that dynamically retrieves user information based on an incoming user ID.

The key part of the implementation is the OData query:

$select=userId,username,firstName,lastName,email&$filter=userId eq '${property.userID}'

This approach reduces unnecessary data retrieval and provides a reusable pattern for integrations that require user-specific information from SuccessFactors.

Thank you for reading. Feel free to share your questions, suggestions, or implementation experiences in the comments.

entry.title: New features in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration packages with the Oct 2026 shipment
entry.content:
We have just shipped new versions of the Pipeline for Cloud Integration packages. Those include couple of feature enhancements but also fixes that were reported.

The following new versions have been shipped:

  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Inbound version 1.0.9
  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Pipelines version 1.0.6
  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Outbound version 1.1.0
  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Templates version 1.2.1

Here the list of new features at a glance:

  • New generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows on Edge Integration Cell: Two new integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI on Edge" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc on Edge" have been added to the Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Outbound package. Deploy and run those flows on Edge Integration Cell if you need to handle XI and/or IDoc outbound scenarios when running the pipeline on Edge Integration Cell. Dedicated flows were needed because the adapter configuration with the proxy type On-Premise is not supported on Edge Integration Cell and hence the corresponding other flows for the Cloud Integration could not be deployed on Edge Integration Cell. For the new flows, currently the proxy type Internet is supported only. The proxy type Manual will be added with one of the next increments but here we depend on development.
  • Exactly Once In Order routing for XI and IDoc inbound processing: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step01 - Inbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step01 - Inbound Processing for Idoc" now support the handling of messages when sent with Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order (EOIO). The approach is to forward EOIO messages to an integration flow whereas you bypass most of the pipeline steps. So, this approach would unblock you as long as the pipeline does not support EOIO from end-to-end. And this way, you can use single point of entries for your XI and IDoc inbound scenarios regardless of the quality of service. You have the option to forward Exactly Once In Order messages either to an exclusive queue or to a ProcessDirect end point. 
  • Generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows supporting receiver with parties: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" now support receiver with party when configuring the XI and IDoc adapters in the Partner Directory.
  • Additional option to override IDoc control record: The integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for IDoc" has been enhanced to be able to maintain the list of IDoc EDIDC control record fields to be overridden by configuring the externalized parameter OverrideControlRecordParameters. With this, you now have three options to maintain the override parameter: via message header in the scenario-specific flow, as string parameter in the Partner Directory, and as externalized parameter of the generic Idoc outbound flow.
  • Disable mandatory IDoc control record fields check: For the integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc", a new configuration parameter EnableControlRecordCheck has been introduced. By default, the parameter is true so that message processing fails if any mandatory control record field is empty or missing. This check has been introduced previously. With the new parameter, you now have the option to disable the check by setting the parameter value to false. In this case, empty mandatory control record fields are ignored and the message processing won't fail in Cloud Integration. You disable the check, when you rather check empty mandatory control record fields in the backend system.
  • Enhanced inbound conversion definition: Sender-specific inbound conversion now supports sender party to determine the endpoint of the scenario-specific inbound conversion flow.
  • Custom pre-processing for standard error handling: The standard error handling has been enhanced supporting custom pre-processing. You now have the option to call a pre-processing custom error flow before calling the standard error handling. Before, it was only possible to replace the standard error handling with your own custom error handling logic. Now, you can stick to the standard error handling and call a custom flow right before the standard error handling is performed. A use case may be to automatically create an incident ticket if maximum number of retries have been exceeded.
  • Custom post-processing: The integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step06 - Outbound Processing" now supports custom exits for post-processing. You have the options to call a custom flow after the message delivery to the next step across all scenarios or scenario-specific without the need to alter the standard flow provided. For latter, you can maintain the string parameters CustomXPostEnabled and CustomXPostEndpoint, repectively, in the Partner Directory. Right now, the CustomXPostEnabled only supports step number 06.
  • Custom pre-transmission: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" now support custom exits for pre-transmission. You have the options to call a custom flow right before the message delivery to the receiving system across all scenarios or scenario-specific without the need to alter the standard flows provided. In addition to the header customXPipelineStep (in this case equals 08), the header customXProtocol (either xi or idoc) is passed to the custom exit flow.
  • Enhanced custom pre-processing setting: The scenario-specific custom exit definition has been enhanced. For each pipeline step, you can now define an own end point by adding the pipeline step number as suffix to the string parameter CustomXPreEndpoint in the Partner Directory.
  • Enhanced allowed headers for custom error handling template: For the "Pipeline v2 Template - Custom Error Handling" template, the allowed headers has been enhanced by adding the regular expression "customX(.*)".
  • Enhanced custom exit template: For the "Pipeline v2 Template - Custom Exit" template, an additional route has been added to support the pipeline step number 08.
  • Supporting slash (/) in sender interface: The integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step01 - Inbound Processing for XI" now supports slash (/) in the sender interface name when using a combination of sender, sender interface and sender interface namespace to determine the partner ID. For the combination of sender and sender interface with fixed ID "SenderInterface", slash (/) was supported before anyway.
  • Supporting slash (/) in receiver interface: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" now support slash (/) in the interface name. When maintaining the configuration parameters in the Partner Directory, the slash (/) needs to be replaced by underscore (_).

The following fixes have been provided:

  • Harden max retry condition: For the "Pipeline v2 Generic Step06 - Outbound Processing" flow, the max retry handling condition was slightly adapted to be more robust avoiding endless message retry. Instead of using equal (=) in the condition, we now use greater or equal than (>=).
  • Type conversion issue: We fixed a bug which resulted into a type conversion exception when in an error case an original message in XML format was stored in the dead letter queue. This happened only for cases where the original XML message was converted into a non-XML message like JSON for instance. The fix was implemented in the restoreMessage script.
  • Wrong condition: We fixed a bug in the integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" with the complex conditions evaluations to route to the corresponding receiver adapters. The condition was hence replaced by a groovy script.

Please update the packages in your Design area to benefit from the changes. We recommend to update your dev and test landscape first and to test there before updating the content on your prod tenant. Though we run extensive regression tests and new feature tests before publishing a new version.

The update of the standard documentation is still work in progress, so stay tuned.

entry.title: MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose CAP API (SCI) via OAuth2JWTBearer Principal Propagation
entry.content:
Introduction/Scenario

This post explains how to configure an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite to securely communicate with CAP API services using OAuth2JWTBearer Assertion. This approach ensures that API access is governed through individual user identities rather than a shared API/technical user, this approach provides better governance, traceability, and compliance.

Important reference: For a detailed explanation of the JWT Bearer Flow App-to-App Authentication setup

  • SAP Help Portal | SAP Online Help
  • Consuming APIs from Other Applications | SAP Help Portal

Previous similar posts

  • MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA ... - SAP Community
  • MCP Server with Integration Suite via API Centric ... - SAP Community

For example, when a user interacts with an AI agent that is connected to the MCP server and accesses CAP APIs, the user should only be able to view and manage data that they are authorized to access. This access is controlled by the user's assigned policies/group under Cloud Identity, ensuring that existing security and governance policies are enforced.

Thanks @MCZL on helping and provide insight on Cloud Identity Services and BAIP/BTP Destination setup. 

 Flow:

→ Agent (Claude/Github Copilot/any AI Agent) 
  → MCP server by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
    → BTP Destination Service (OAuth2JWTBearer) 
        → CAP Service APIs (executed as the authenticated user)

Note: 

  1. The MCP server uses SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) as its authentication provider instead of the default XSUAA, as the target APIs are also protected by SAP Cloud Identity Services. Directly accessing an IAS-protected resource through an XSUAA-based authentication flow don't seem feasible.
  2. This approach limits to a single client ID allowed to access the MCP server access This restriction exists because the BAIP/BTP destination configuration requires the consumer's client ID to be specified rather than the provider's client ID. In this scenario, the consumer is the Integration Suite MCP server, while the provider is the CAP service.
  3. However, you can directly use the provider client ID for the Integration Suite MCP and the Destination setup, skip on creating a separate SAP Cloud Identity Service instance as Consumer, however the restriction - Single client ID still applied on this. This writing is demonstrating how to use separate SAP Cloud Identity Service instance as Consumer to call the CAP API (as Provider).
  4. OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion can also be used in this scenario. However, this authentication flow is typically designed for communication between Cloud Foundry applications - SAML Bearer Assertion Flow between Cloud Foundry Applications | SAP Help Portal

Pre-requisite:

  • SAP BAIP/BTP with Cloud Foundry Enabled
  • SAP Integration Suite with MCP server, Integration Cell runtime capability
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS)
  • AI Agent able to communicate with MCP server

1. CAP Services creation and deploy

This demo is using a CAP bookshop sample (without the UI deployment) as the MCP server will only access the CAP API services. 

Note: You may use any AI Model to assist on CAP app generation, ensure you connect to the CAP MCP server for more accurate response.

Navigate to the project folder in terminal and execute the commands below

cds add ams
cds add hana
npm install
cds build --for ams
cds add mta

Update the MTA file - to include the additional grant type and binding options

2. Setup Consumer and Provider in Cloud Identity Services

entry.title: Automating Referral Bonus Payouts: RCM to EC
entry.content:
Introduction & Business Problem

Employee referral programs are among the most effective recruitment channels for organizations. However, managing the end-to-end operational lifecycle from tracking candidate referrals in Recruiting Management (RCM) to paying out referral bonuses in Employee Central (EC) often involves significant manual administration.

In a standard setup:

  • Referrals are captured within Recruiting Management (RCM).
  • The candidate is hired.
  • HR or payroll teams manually pull reports, calculate milestone eligibility (e.g., 3 months post-hire, passed probation etc), and import spreadsheets into Employee Central (EC) as non-recurring payments.

This manual handover creates operational bottlenecks, delayed payouts, and tracking discrepancies.

In this blog, we walk through an end-to-end, and fully automated solution that bridges the gap between RCM and EC using Custom Metadata Framework (MDF) Objects, Associations, and Integration Center jobs eliminating external middleware and manual imports. 

High-Level Solution Architecture

Step-by-Step Implementation

Step 1: Define Referral Amount and Payment Date Logic

Before configuring the integration, decide how your organization determines bonus amounts and payout timing. 

  • Where should the Referral Amount live?

    Job Requisitions include a standard referral bonus field. If your payout is tied to the position/hiring country, keeping it on the requisition template is the easiest way to track and adjust values per role. However, if your payout is based on the referrer's country, you don't need it on the requisition you can calculate it on the fly using a business rule or integration logic.

  • When should the bonus be paid?

    Payment timing is fully flexible. Depending on your business policy, it can be scheduled immediately after the candidate finishes probation, based on a fixed timeline (such as 3 or 6 months after the hire date), or customized by region.

 

Step 2: Configure Custom MDF Tracking Objects

To handle one referrer referring multiple applicants, configure a Parent-Child (Composite) MDF relationship under Configure Object Definitions:

Navigate to Configure Object Definition -- Create New -- Object Definition.

1. Parent Object: cust_ParentReferralTracking

2. Child Object: cust_ChildReferralTracking

Create Child object and add required fields

 

Associate the child object with parent object

 

Step 3: Create Pay Component

Navigate to Manage Organisation, Pay and Job Structures and create a non recurring pay component to capture Referral Amount in EC.

Step 4: Add MDF Object on employee profile.

Navigate to Manage Configuration UI - Create New -- Select Parent Referral Object. Update the required fields, labels, UI etc and Save.

Navigate to Configure Latest People Profile, Add Category, add the Object and save it.

This will add a card on employee profile which provide all referral information.

Step 5: Grant Permissions

Navigate to Manage Permission Roles to provide appropriate access to the newly created MDF objects and pay component and the employee referral card created.

Step 6: Build Integration Center Job 1 (RCM to Custom MDF)

This job extracts referral details for successfully hired candidates and stages them in our custom MDF.

  • Source Starting Entity: CandidateEmployeeReferral.

  • Target Entities: cust_ParentReferralTracking and composite child cust_ChildReferralTracking.

Map the fields correctly and add a filter on candidate status, that only Hired candidates should be considered and referred one.

 

Step 7: Build Integration Center Job 2 (MDF to One-Time Payment)

This scheduled integration evaluates records in the custom tracking object and creates spot bonus payouts in EC.

  • Source Starting Entity: cust_ChildReferralTracking.

  • Target Entity: EmpPayCompNonRecurring (Spot Bonus)

Step 8: Job Scheduling & Sequencing

To ensure data integrity, schedule the two Integration Center jobs in sequential order with a buffer of at least 2 to 3 hours:

  • First Job (RCM -- MDF): Populates and updates the custom referral tracking records.
  • Second Job (MDF -- EC): Triggers a few hours later to read the updated MDF data and create the one-time payments.

Below are previews of how the data looks once the solution is running end-to-end.


Key Advantages of This Design

  • Full Operational Transparency: HR administrators and managers can view referral progression directly on MDF portlets without querying recruitment pipelines.
  • Zero Middleware Dependency: Accomplished 100% natively within SAP SuccessFactors using standard Integration Center capabilities—no external middleware (SAP Integration Suite / CPI) licenses required.
  • Audit Trail: Because notes and job requisition IDs are linked into EmpPayCompNonRecurring,  payroll and compensation teams maintain complete visibility into payment origins.
  • Employees gain transparency into referral progress directly on their People Profile.

Conclusion

Connecting Recruiting Management to Employee Central using MDF objects and Integration Center turns a manual, error-prone spreadsheet routine into a seamless automated process. Best of all, this solution requires zero external middleware or extra licensing, running 100% within SAP SuccessFactors.

Thanks for reading! Have you implemented a similar setup, or do you handle milestone payouts differently? Share your thoughts, questions, or feedback in the comments below.

Happy optimizing and happy learning! 🙂

entry.title: Best Practices Pipeline for Cloud Integration: How to deal with slash in the interface name
entry.content:
In the latest announcement New features in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration packages with the Oct 2026 shipment about the new Pipeline for Cloud Integration version, you may have seen that we added further support for slash (/) in the interface name and you may wonder what this is all about.

Well, there are some character restrictions of the Partner Directory that we heavily use to dynamically configure the configuration scenarios for messages running through the pipeline. For some use cases, you need to enter the interface name into an alternative partner or for defining a string parameter. The scheme of an alternative partner and the ID of a string parameter do not support special characters such as slash (/). Hence, the issue occurs if your interface name contains a slash (/) which is not so uncommon when exchanging IDoc messages for instance.

The general approach to overcome this restriction is to replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_) if you configure Partner Directory fields that do not support the special characters. During message processing, your interface name can contain special characters. However, to read the Partner Directory string parameters or to determine your partner ID, the special characters are automatically replaced with an underscore (_) in the flow scripts and can therefore be matched with the Partner Directory settings.

Note, that the value of a string parameter and the ID of an alternative partner do support slash (/). So, here you must not replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_).

What are the use cases where this approach needs to be applied?

  • For incoming messages, we need to determine the partner ID based on an alternative partner. In most cases, the sender system name and the sender interface name is sufficient to unambiguously determine the partner ID. In this case, we use a constant term for the Scheme of the alternative partner and hence won't be impacted by the character restriction. However, if the combination of sender system name and sender interface name alone is not sufficient and it becomes unambiguous only together with the sender interface namespace, then the Scheme of your alternative partner needs to hold the sender interface name. If now your sender interface name contains a slash (/), then this needs to be replaced with an underscore (_). See Partner ID.
  • For outgoing messages using either the generic XI outbound processing flow or the generic IDoc outbound processing flow, you have the option to configure the XI/IDoc connection parameters and the scenario parameters using the Partner Directory. Here, for some of your settings the string parameters may contain the receiver interface name. If now your receiver interface name contains a slash (/), then this needs to be replaced with an underscore (_). See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

Inbound use case where slash (/) must not be replaced

If possible, define the alternative partner as a combination of the sender system name and the sender interface name. In this case, the alternative partner is defined as follows:

  • Agency holds the sender system name
  • Scheme is constant "SenderInterface"
  • ID equals the sender interface name

As you can see, for this option we must not replace the slash (/) of the sender interface name because the ID of the alternative partner supports special characters.

Inbound use case where slash (/) needs to be replaced

If you need the sender interface namespace to make the key unambiguous, you need to define the alternative partner as follows:

  • Agency holds the sender system name
  • Scheme equals the sender interface name
  • ID equals the sender interface namespace

As you can see, for this option you must replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_) when maintaining the Scheme. In our case, the sender interface name is actually /SI_PurchaseOrder/Create/Outbound/Async. I have to admit that for test purposes, this name is a bit constructed. But a real customer case is to use the XI adapter to exchange IDoc messages that contain a slash (/)  in the IDoc type and message type.

If you run the scenario, you can see in the message monitoring that the sender interface name contains couple of slashes (/). During message processing the slashes (/) were replaced with underscore (_),  and the partner ID was successfully identified.

Outbound use case where slash (/) needs to be replaced

To configure the XI or IDoc outbound, you have three options: via message headers in the scenario-specific flow, via externalized parameters of the generic XI/IDoc outbound processing flow or via configuration in the Partner Directory. For latter option, if your receiver interface name contains a slash (/) and the string parameter ID requires to add the receiver interface name as suffix, you need to replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_).

In below example, we configure the IDoc outbound. Here, we like to override the control header parameters RCVPOR, RCVPRN, SNDPOR, and SNDPRN for the receiver interface /FLIGHTBOOK_CREATE./FLIGHTBOOK_CREATE01. When we add the receiver interface name as suffix, the slash (/) needs to be replaced.

If you run the scenario, you can see in the message monitoring that the control headers have been properly defined and the outbound processing has been successfully completed.

For a complete list of parameters for the generic IDoc outbound processing flow, see IDoc Receiver Adapter. For the generic XI outbound processing flow, see XI Receiver Adapter.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 1: Setting up CTMS in Central
entry.content:
Part 1 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 0 we drew the map: Content Agent packs the parcel, CTMS delivers it, a second Content Agent unpacks it. In this part we build the delivery service itself: CTMS in the Central subaccount, with two stops (nodes) and the road between them (a route).

 

Step 1: Subscribe to CTMS

In the Central subaccount, go to Services > Service Marketplace, find Cloud Transport Management and create a subscription. The subscription is the screen people work in.

Then, in Security > Role Collections, create a role collection with the CTMS role Administrator and assign it to your user. Without it the app may open, but you cannot create nodes or routes.

Step 2: Create a service instance and a key

The subscription is for people. Other services need their own door. In the same subaccount, create a service instance of Cloud Transport Management with plan standard, then create a service key on it.

The key holds four values we need later: the address (uri), the login (clientid and clientsecret) and the token server (uaa.url). In Part 2 these go into the Dev destination TransportManagementService.

Treat the key like a password. Do not paste it in tickets or screenshots.

Step 3: Create the source node

Open the CTMS app, go to Transport Nodes and click +.

  • Name: something clear, for example SOURCE_NODE. Write it down: Part 2 uses this exact name.
  • Tick Allow Upload to Node. This lets Content Agent in Dev drop parcels here.
  • Leave content type and destination empty. Nothing is ever imported into a source node.

Step 4: Create the target node

  • Name: for example TARGET_NODE.
  • Content Type: Multi-Target Application. That is the parcel format Content Agent produces.
  • Destination: leave it empty for now. Part 3 creates CAS_on_Target, the connection to the Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, and we come back to fill it in.
  • Forward Mode: keep the default. It only matters when there is another node after this one.

Step 5: Create the route

Go to Transport Routes, click +, give it a name, pick the source node and the target node, and save. That is all a route is: "parcels from here go there".

 

Left: creating a node (names blurred). Right: creating the route.

Check it

Open Landscape Visualization. You should see two boxes joined by an arrow. If the arrow is missing, the route was not saved with both nodes.

Roles for this part

WhoNeedsFor
You, building the landscapeCTMS role Administrator, in a role collectionCreating nodes and routes
Whoever imports laterCTMS role ImportOperator, in a role collectionClicking Import on the target node (Part 4)

The full list for every service is in Part 7.

What tripped me up in my setup

These are from my own project log, not from the documentation.

  • The cockpit shortcut does not work across subaccounts. The key lives in Central, but the destination that uses it (Part 2) lives in Dev. The "Create from Service Instance" option on the Destinations screen only sees keys in its own subaccount, so I had to copy the values from the key by hand.
  • That hand copy caused my first real error. The client ID in my destination did not match the key, and Content Agent could not reach CTMS until I copied it again. My advice: create a fresh key and copy all four values from it in one go, never from an older key or a note.
  • Old instances cost me time. Earlier tutorial attempts had left two CTMS instances (and several other duplicates in different spaces) in my landscape, and I had to work out which key belonged to which. Keep one CTMS instance per landscape, give it a clear name, and note which space it is in.
  • Choose the source node name once. Part 2 needs it character for character, so decide the final name before you create the node.

What comes next

CTMS is ready but empty. In Part 2 we switch to the Dev subaccount, set up Content Agent and create the three fixed-name destinations, using the service key from step 2 and the source node name from step 3.

Master the Pipeline Concept in SAP Cloud Integration through our Live Webinar Series

Are you working with SAP Cloud Integration and looking to streamline how you build, operate, and migrate your integration scenarios. If so, we are running a free 3-part live webinar series in November dedicated entirely to the Pipeline Concept in SAP Cloud Integration - and it is available to all SAP customers through their Foundational Success Plan.

Whether you are new to the Pipeline concept or already running integrations and looking to deepen your operational knowledge, this series takes you from the fundamentals through to hands-on setup, real-world migration, and a comparison of when the Pipeline approach is and is not the right choice for your landscape.

Why the Pipeline Concept Matters

Integration development in SAP Cloud Integration has historically involved building individual, often bespoke integration flows for each scenario. The Pipeline concept changes this by introducing a reusable, standardised architecture that separates generic processing logic from scenario-specific content. The result is less development effort, lower maintenance overhead, and reduced integration costs across your landscape without sacrificing flexibility.

These sessions explain the what, the why, and the how including what happens when something goes wrong, and how to recover.

The session concludes with an open Q&A across all three weeks' content for your chance to get direct answers from the experts.

What you will learn:

  • The key stages of a migration scenario from source interface to deployment
  • A comparison of Pipeline and non-Pipeline implementation approaches and their differences
  • The benefits and trade-offs of each approach
